query.original_query: LLM safety representations transfer across languages low-resource multilingual jailbreak internal harmfulness

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representations of safety and harmfulness in multilingual LLMs, whether safety features transfer across languages, probing safety-related neurons and attention heads in low-resource language jailbreak scenarios
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether internal representations of safety and harmfulness in multilingual large language models transfer across languages, particularly in low-resource language jailbreak scenarios. Using activation patching and causal tracing, we analyze the role of specific MLP layers and attention heads in mediating refusal behavior when harmful prompts are translated from high-resource to low-resource languages. Our analysis reveals that safety-related features, identified through sparse probing of the residual stream, are largely localized to English-centric circuits and exhibit degraded activation in low-resource languages. We find that feature steering interventions effective in English fail to elicit refusal in languages with limited pretraining data, suggesting that monosemantic safety features do not fully transfer. Results show that attention heads in later layers, which encode harmfulness detection in English, become polysemantic or inactive for low-resource inputs. These findings indicate that current alignment techniques produce language-specific safety representations, leaving vulnerabilities in multilingual deployment.

sub_queries.semantic_query: LLM safety representations transfer across languages low-resource multilingual jailbreak internal harmfulness
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether internal representations of harmfulness in large language models transfer across languages, particularly from high-resource to low-resource languages, and whether this facilitates multilingual jailbreak attacks. Using probing classifiers applied to hidden states from a multilingual transformer-based model, we measured the linear separability of harmful versus harmless content across English, Spanish, Hindi, and Swahili. Results indicate that safety-relevant features learned in high-resource languages partially generalize to low-resource languages, but with significantly reduced alignment. Specifically, probes trained on English internal representations show degraded performance when evaluated on Swahili and Hindi, suggesting that safety mechanisms are less robust for languages underrepresented in the training corpus. Further analysis using representation similarity analysis reveals that the model’s internal geometry for harmfulness diverges across language families. Findings support the hypothesis that cross-linguistic transfer of safety representations is incomplete, creating a vulnerability surface for jailbreak attempts in low-resource languages. These results highlight the need for language-specific safety alignment during multilingual model training.

papers.title: Who Transfers Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cross-lingual safety alignment in LLMs, specifically identifying a sparse set of shared safety neurons that regulate safety behavior across languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a sparse set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons) that regulate safety behavior across languages and proposes a neuron-oriented training strategy that selectively fine-tunes these neurons to improve safety in low-resource languages without degrading general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that cross-lingual safety alignment can be achieved by identifying and selectively fine-tuning a sparse set of shared safety neurons, which improves safety in low-resource languages while minimizing the alignment tax.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs contain monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) that are causally responsible for safety refusal behavior.
The subset of MS-Neurons shared between high-resource and low-resource languages (SS-Neurons) serves as a bridge for cross-lingual safety transfer.
Suppressing SS-Neurons causes concurrent safety drops across low-resource languages, while reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency.
The proposed SS-Neuron expansion strategy, which fine-tunes only the English MS-Neurons using parallel safety data, significantly reduces attack success rates in low-resource languages while preserving model utility.
The method is parameter-efficient, updating less than 0.6% of parameters, and outperforms state-of-the-art safety alignment methods.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on safety-oriented tasks, and the applicability to general-purpose tasks remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validate the neuron-level intervention across non-safety domains to transfer complex cognitive skills.
papers.abstract: Multilingual safety remains significantly imbalanced, leaving non-high-resource (NHR) languages vulnerable compared to robust high-resource (HR) ones. Moreover, the neural mechanisms driving safety alignment remain unclear despite observed cross-lingual representation transfer. In this paper, we find that LLMs contain a set of cross-lingual shared safety neurons (SS-Neurons), a remarkably small yet critical neuronal subset that jointly regulates safety behavior across languages. We first identify monolingual safety neurons (MS-Neurons) and validate their causal role in safety refusal behavior through targeted activation and suppression. Our cross-lingual analyses then identify SS-Neurons as the subset of MS-Neurons shared between HR and NHR languages, serving as a bridge to transfer safety capabilities from HR to NHR domains. We observe that suppressing these neurons causes concurrent safety drops across NHR languages, whereas reinforcing them improves cross-lingual defensive consistency. Building on these insights, we propose a simple neuron-oriented training strategy that targets SS-Neurons based on language resource distribution and model architecture. Experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning this tiny neuronal subset outperforms state-of-the-art methods, significantly enhancing NHR safety while maintaining the model's general capabilities. The code and dataset will be available athttps://github.com/1518630367/SS-Neuron-Expansion.

papers.title: SafeNeuron: Neuron-Level Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms underlie model safety, and how can we make these mechanisms stable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that redistributes safety representations across the network to improve robustness against neuron-level attacks while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment, demonstrating that robust safety requires distributed and redundant representations rather than reliance on a small set of fragile parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Safety behaviors in aligned models are concentrated in a small subset of neurons, making alignment brittle and vulnerable to neuron-level attacks.
SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks and reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators.
SafeNeuron preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) without introducing over-refusal.
Layer-wise and cross-task analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations, including a core set of neurons active across diverse harmful tasks.
Iterative application of SafeNeuron progressively redistributes safety behaviors, constructing redundant safety pathways.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs are typically safety-aligned before release to prevent harmful content generation. However, recent studies show that safety behaviors are concentrated in a small subset of parameters, making alignment brittle and easily bypassed through neuron-level attacks. Moreover, most existing alignment methods operate at the behavioral level, offering limited control over the model's internal safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that improves robustness by redistributing safety representations across the network. SafeNeuron first identifies safety-related neurons, then freezes these neurons during preference optimization to prevent reliance on sparse safety pathways and force the model to construct redundant safety representations. Extensive experiments across models and modalities demonstrate that SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks, reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators, and preserves general capabilities. Furthermore, our layer-wise analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations. Overall, SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: NLSR: Neuron-Level Safety Realignment of Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we restore the safety of large language models after harmful fine-tuning without requiring additional training, by focusing on neuron-level updates?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, neuron-level safety realignment framework that restores model safety by identifying and patching safety-critical neurons based on similarity differences before and after fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron-level safety realignment is an effective, training-free approach to restore safety in LLMs after harmful fine-tuning, without disrupting the task-specific optimization process.
papers.key_findings:
NLSR effectively restores safety in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks while maintaining task-level accuracy.
Safety-critical neurons show noticeable similarity differences after fine-tuning, which can be corrected by transplanting neurons from a reference model.
Adaptive safety-critical layer pruning is necessary for identifying safety-compromised layers.
After safety pre-amplification, various safety neuron identification methods (Wanda, SNIP, and the proposed method) show high similarity in localizing safety-critical neurons.
The method is decoupled from the fine-tuning phase and requires no additional training.
papers.abstract: The emergence of finetuning-as-a-service has revealed a new vulnerability in large language models (LLMs). A mere handful of malicious data uploaded by users can subtly manipulate the finetuning process, resulting in an alignment-broken model. Existing methods to counteract fine-tuning attacks typically require substantial computational resources. Even with parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA, gradient updates remain essential. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{N}euron-\textbf{L}evel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{R}ealignment (\textbf{NLSR}), a training-free framework that restores the safety of LLMs based on the similarity difference of safety-critical neurons before and after fine-tuning. The core of our framework is first to construct a safety reference model from an initially aligned model to amplify safety-related features in neurons. We then utilize this reference model to identify safety-critical neurons, which we prepare as patches. Finally, we selectively restore only those neurons that exhibit significant similarity differences by transplanting these prepared patches, thereby minimally altering the fine-tuned model. Extensive experiments demonstrate significant safety enhancements in fine-tuned models across multiple downstream tasks, while greatly maintaining task-level accuracy. Our findings suggest regions of some safety-critical neurons show noticeable differences after fine-tuning, which can be effectively corrected by transplanting neurons from the reference model without requiring additional training. The code will be available at \url{https://github.com/xinykou/NLSR}

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: What is the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ships and Sahara to identify safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, showing that ablating a small number of these heads significantly reduces model safety.
papers.conclusion: Ships and Sahara provide a novel perspective for interpreting safety in LLMs, revealing that specific attention heads are crucial for safety and are sparsely distributed.
papers.key_findings:
Safety attention heads are sparse; ablating them significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR).
Safety heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety.
Models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads.
Ablating safety heads has minimal impact on model helpfulness.
The proposed method localizes safety parameters at a finer granularity (head-level) compared to prior work.
future_direction: Exploring the association between attention heads and other safety capabilities beyond direct rejection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leaves a Trace: Understanding and Detecting Jailbreak Attacks from Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal representations of LLMs differ between jailbreak and benign prompts, and can these differences be used for detection and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak prompts leave identifiable traces in internal representations; a tensor-based framework can detect and mitigate jailbreaks by bypassing susceptible layers without model fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations contain strong and consistent signals for jailbreak detection and mitigation, providing a lightweight, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak and benign prompts exhibit distinct layer-dependent latent signatures in internal representations.
These signatures can be uncovered using tensor decomposition and used for detection with high F1 scores.
Layer-wise susceptibility scores can identify layers that strongly encode jailbreak features.
Bypassing susceptible layers at inference time can block 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving 94% of benign prompts.
The patterns are consistent across diverse model families (transformer and state-space models).
papers.limitation: Persona- or roleplay-based prompt injections can persist even after bypassing susceptible layers, and the fixed probability threshold for bypassing may not capture attacks that distribute influence across multiple layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to additional attack families (e.g., GCG, PAIR) by incorporating corresponding prompt distributions during factor learning.
Adopting adaptive or cumulative susceptibility criteria for layer bypass.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a critical security challenge with the widespread deployment of conversational AI systems. Adversarial users exploit these models through carefully crafted prompts to elicit restricted or unsafe outputs, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Jailbreaking. Despite numerous proposed defense mechanisms, attackers continue to develop adaptive prompting strategies, and existing models remain vulnerable. This motivates approaches that examine the internal behavior of LLMs rather than relying solely on prompt-level defenses. In this work, we study jailbreaking from both security and interpretability perspectives by analyzing how internal representations differ between jailbreak and benign prompts. We conduct a systematic layer-wise analysis across multiple open-source models, including GPT-J, LLaMA, Mistral, and the state-space model Mamba, and identify consistent latent-space patterns associated with harmful inputs. We then propose a tensor-based latent representation framework that captures structure in hidden activations and enables lightweight jailbreak detection without model fine-tuning or auxiliary LLM-based detectors. We further demonstrate that the latent signals can be used to actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time. On an abliterated LLaMA-3.1-8B model, selectively bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks 78% of jailbreak attempts while preserving benign behavior on 94% of benign prompts. This intervention operates entirely at inference time and introduces minimal overhead, providing a scalable foundation for achieving stronger coverage by incorporating additional attack distributions or more refined susceptibility thresholds. Our results provide evidence that jailbreak behavior is rooted in identifiable internal structures and suggest a complementary, architecture-agnostic direction for improving LLM security.

papers.title: AISA: Awakening Intrinsic Safety Awareness in Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks in large language models by awakening their intrinsic safety awareness without fine-tuning or external modules?
papers.core_contribution: AISA is a lightweight defense framework that extracts intrinsic safety signals from attention head activations via linear probing and uses them to steer generation through logits adjustment, achieving robust jailbreak defense without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: AISA provides an effective, lightweight defense against jailbreak attacks by leveraging intrinsic safety awareness in LLMs, offering a resource-efficient alternative to safety alignment tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs possess intrinsic safety awareness even without safety-specific fine-tuning, as evidenced by refusal behavior in uncensored models.
Attention head outputs, particularly at the final structural token before generation, provide the strongest discriminative signal for prompt intent.
AISA's data-driven head selection and logits steering outperform existing defense baselines in safety and utility preservation across diverse jailbreak datasets.
The safety awareness signal is architecture-dependent and persists across alignment variants, indicating a common pretrained basis.
AISA enables unaligned models to match or exceed the safety performance of aligned counterparts while avoiding over-refusal.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that elicit harmful or policy-violating outputs, while many existing defenses rely on expensive fine-tuning, intrusive prompt rewriting, or external guardrails that add latency and can degrade helpfulness. We present AISA, a lightweight, single-pass defense that activates safety behaviors already latent inside the model rather than treating safety as an add-on. AISA first localizes intrinsic safety awareness via spatiotemporal analysis and shows that intent-discriminative signals are broadly encoded, with especially strong separability appearing in the scaled dot-product outputs of specific attention heads near the final structural tokens before generation. Using a compact set of automatically selected heads, AISA extracts an interpretable prompt-risk score with minimal overhead, achieving detector-level performance competitive with strong proprietary baselines on small (7B) models. AISA then performs logits-level steering: it modulates the decoding distribution in proportion to the inferred risk, ranging from normal generation for benign prompts to calibrated refusal for high-risk requests -- without changing model parameters, adding auxiliary modules, or requiring multi-pass inference. Extensive experiments spanning 13 datasets, 12 LLMs, and 14 baselines demonstrate that AISA improves robustness and transfer while preserving utility and reducing false refusals, enabling safer deployment even for weakly aligned or intentionally risky model variants.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment work in large language models from a mechanistic perspective, and can we identify specific neurons (safety neurons) responsible for safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies sparse safety neurons in LLMs that are causally responsible for safety behaviors, and shows that patching these neurons can restore safety performance. It also explains alignment tax by showing that safety and helpfulness share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a mechanistic understanding of safety alignment through safety neurons, demonstrating their causal role, transferability, and application in safeguards, paving the way for more robust alignment algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (about 5% of neurons) and causally effective, with patching restoring over 90% of safety performance.
Safety neurons encode transferable mechanisms, effective across multiple red-teaming benchmarks without sacrificing general ability.
Safety neurons are robust to training randomness, with high overlap across different training runs.
Alignment tax arises because safety and helpfulness alignment share overlapping neurons but require different activation patterns for the same neurons.
Safety neurons can be used to build an effective safeguard that detects unsafe outputs before generation, improving model safety.
papers.limitation:
Safety neurons require activations from already aligned models; training-free methods to obtain these activations are not explored.
The alignment used (IA)3, a parameter-efficient method, while real-world models often undergo full fine-tuning; the impact of this difference is unknown.
The paper identifies which neurons affect safety but not how they exert this influence.
future_direction: Exploring training-free methods to obtain safety neuron activations.
Investigating how safety neurons exert their influence (the specific mechanisms).
Studying the evolution of safety neurons during pre-training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel in various capabilities but pose safety risks such as generating harmful content and misinformation, even after safety alignment. In this paper, we explore the inner mechanisms of safety alignment through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, focusing on identifying and analyzing safety neurons within LLMs that are responsible for safety behaviors. We propose inference-time activation contrasting to locate these neurons and dynamic activation patching to evaluate their causal effects on model safety. Experiments on multiple prevalent LLMs demonstrate that we can consistently identify about $5\%$ safety neurons, and by only patching their activations we can restore over $90\%$ of the safety performance across various red-teaming benchmarks without influencing general ability. The finding of safety neurons also helps explain the ''alignment tax'' phenomenon by revealing that the key neurons for model safety and helpfulness significantly overlap, yet they require different activation patterns for the same neurons. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application of our findings in safeguarding LLMs by detecting unsafe outputs before generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/SafetyNeuron.

papers.title: Foot In The Door: Understanding Large Language Model Jailbreaking via Cognitive Psychology
papers.research_question: How can cognitive psychology explain the decision-making mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) during jailbreaking attacks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a psychological explanation for LLM jailbreaking using cognitive consistency theory and proposes a new automated jailbreaking method called FITD based on the Foot-in-the-Door technique.
papers.conclusion: This paper explains existing jailbreaking methods from a psychological perspective and proposes a novel jailbreaking method using the foot-in-the-door technique, aiming to offer a new approach to understanding LLMs' thought processes and inspire future alignment work.
papers.key_findings:
FITD achieves an average success rate of 83.9% on 8 advanced LLMs.
FITD is particularly effective on Claude series models compared to other jailbreaking methods.
Hate speech and harassment/threat categories have lower attack success rates and require more dialogue steps for jailbreaking.
Recursive splitting of prompts increases jailbreak success rate.
Initial splitting methods that include background and character settings improve the effectiveness of jailbreaking.
papers.limitation:
The types of malicious questions and jailbreaking prompt words may not be comprehensive enough.
The prompt splitting instance is manually designed, and potentially better alternatives exist.
The method has only been tested in English and has not been extended to other languages.
The psychological explanation does not apply to jailbreak prompts with uninterpreted strings.
future_direction: Continue to delve into the psychological characteristics of LLMs, particularly focusing on cognitive and social psychology mechanisms.
Develop LLM adversarial training techniques based on psychological theories to enhance alignment at the psychological level.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gradually become the gateway for people to acquire new knowledge. However, attackers can break the model's security protection ("jail") to access restricted information, which is called "jailbreaking." Previous studies have shown the weakness of current LLMs when confronted with such jailbreaking attacks. Nevertheless, comprehension of the intrinsic decision-making mechanism within the LLMs upon receipt of jailbreak prompts is noticeably lacking. Our research provides a psychological explanation of the jailbreak prompts. Drawing on cognitive consistency theory, we argue that the key to jailbreak is guiding the LLM to achieve cognitive coordination in an erroneous direction. Further, we propose an automatic black-box jailbreaking method based on the Foot-in-the-Door (FITD) technique. This method progressively induces the model to answer harmful questions via multi-step incremental prompts. We instantiated a prototype system to evaluate the jailbreaking effectiveness on 8 advanced LLMs, yielding an average success rate of 83.9%. This study builds a psychological perspective on the explanatory insights into the intrinsic decision-making logic of LLMs.

papers.title: Unraveling LLM Jailbreaks Through Safety Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, and how can we defend against them by understanding and manipulating safety-related knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neuron-level interpretability method for safety knowledge and a fine-tuning defense (SafeTuning) that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Safety knowledge neurons play a critical role in defending against jailbreak attacks, and the proposed methods offer a new perspective for understanding and enhancing LLM security.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related knowledge neurons in MLP layers can be interpreted by projecting their activations into a vocabulary space, revealing distinct 'Rejection' and 'Conformity' patterns.
Calibrating the activation of safety neurons (ActCali) can control model behavior, achieving over 97% attack success rate in making aligned models comply with harmful requests.
Fine-tuning only the identified safety-critical neurons and their activation pathways (SafeTuning) significantly reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and jailbreak methods.
Isolating safety-critical neurons is crucial for maintaining model utility when performing activation adjustments or fine-tuning for defense.
papers.limitation:
Primarily investigates well-aligned models, leaving the challenge of effectively aligning non-aligned models largely unexplored.
Focus is on Large Language Models; extending these alignment techniques to emerging multi-modal LLMs remains an open problem.
The proposed methods require manual tuning of hyperparameters; developing automated techniques is an important future direction.
future_direction: Extending alignment techniques to non-aligned models.
Applying the methods to multi-modal LLMs.
Developing automated techniques to identify and adapt hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly attracting attention in various applications. Nonetheless, there is a growing concern as some users attempt to exploit these models for malicious purposes, including the synthesis of controlled substances and the propagation of disinformation, a technique known as "Jailbreak." While some studies have achieved defenses against jailbreak attacks by modifying output distributions or detecting harmful content, the exact rationale still remains elusive. In this work, we present a novel neuron-level interpretability method that focuses on the role of safety-related knowledge neurons. Unlike existing approaches, our method projects the model's internal representation into a more consistent and interpretable vocabulary space. We then show that adjusting the activation of safety-related neurons can effectively control the model's behavior with a mean ASR higher than 97%. Building on this insight, we propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to improve model robustness against jailbreaks. SafeTuning consistently reduces attack success rates across multiple LLMs and outperforms all four baseline defenses. These findings offer a new perspective on understanding and defending against jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Spot Risks Before Speaking! Unraveling Safety Attention Heads in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can internal activations of large vision-language models, specifically attention heads, be used to detect malicious prompts and understand inner safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Discovers safety attention heads in LVLMs that can detect malicious prompts and constructs an efficient, tuning-free defender (SAHs) based on these heads.
papers.conclusion: Leveraging safety attention heads effectively protects LVLMs from malicious prompts with minimal inference overhead, as confirmed by experiments across various attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Activations from attention heads can linearly separate malicious prompts from benign ones.
Sparse attention heads generate strongly discriminative features for identifying malicious inputs.
Safety heads act as specialized shields; ablating them reduces model safety without affecting utility.
The reduced number of safety heads in LVLMs increases their vulnerability compared to LLMs.
The constructed detector using safety heads shows strong zero-shot generalization capabilities.
papers.abstract: With the integration of an additional modality, large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit greater vulnerability to safety risks (e.g., jailbreaking) compared to their language-only predecessors. Although recent studies have devoted considerable effort to the post-hoc alignment of LVLMs, the inner safety mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we discover that internal activations of LVLMs during the first token generation can effectively identify malicious prompts across different attacks. This inherent safety perception is governed by sparse attention heads, which we term ``safety heads." Further analysis reveals that these heads act as specialized shields against malicious prompts; ablating them leads to higher attack success rates, while the model's utility remains unaffected. By locating these safety heads and concatenating their activations, we construct a straightforward but powerful malicious prompt detector that integrates seamlessly into the generation process with minimal extra inference overhead. Despite its simple structure of a logistic regression model, the detector surprisingly exhibits strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. Experiments across various prompt-based attacks confirm the effectiveness of leveraging safety heads to protect LVLMs. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Ziwei-Zheng/SAHs}.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Soteria: Language-Specific Functional Parameter Steering for Multilingual Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we ensure consistent safety across multiple languages in large language models by locating and minimally adjusting language-specific functional parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Soteria, a lightweight method that identifies and adjusts language-specific functional attention heads to improve multilingual safety alignment by modifying only ~3% of parameters, reducing harmful outputs without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: Soteria provides an effective, parameter-efficient path to scalable multilingual safety alignment, enhancing model safety across diverse languages without compromising utility.
papers.key_findings:
Soteria significantly reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages on safety benchmarks like MultiJail and XThreatBench.
The method outperforms baseline safety alignment techniques such as Safety Arithmetic, Resta, and TIES.
Modifying only the O-projection weights of identified functional heads preserves general model capabilities, as shown by stable MMLU scores.
Attention head analysis reveals that high- and mid-resource languages share functional heads in mid-layers, while low-resource languages utilize heads in later layers.
The approach is robust against state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks like POATE and RDR.
papers.limitation:
Relies on per-language functional neuron identification, which requires accurate language segmentation and task-based data in each target language; resource constraints and data limitations can reduce selection precision.
Does not guarantee comprehensive coverage of every cultural nuance or emergent harmful behavior.
future_direction: Investigating attention-head analysis to tackle task-specific heads, misalignment, and hallucination issues.
Enhancing universal attention heads to improve cross-lingual understanding and zero-shot performance for underrepresented languages.
Refining or shifting the latent space of problematic heads to improve overall alignment and trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Ensuring consistent safety across multiple languages remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs). We introduce Soteria, a lightweight yet powerful strategy that locates and minimally adjusts the "functional heads" most responsible for harmful content generation in each language. By altering only a fraction of parameters, Soteria drastically reduces policy violations without sacrificing overall model performance, even in low-resource settings. To rigorously evaluate our approach, we also present XThreatBench, a specialized multilingual dataset capturing fine-grained harmful behaviors drawn from real policy guidelines. Experiments with leading open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral) show that Soteria consistently improves safety metrics across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. These findings highlight a promising path toward scalable, linguistically attuned, and ethically aligned LLMs worldwide.

papers.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just A Few Attention Heads
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why safety alignment in large language models is vulnerable to jailbreak attacks due to the concentration of safety mechanisms in a few attention heads, and whether distributing these mechanisms across more heads can enhance robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RDSHA to identify safety-critical attention heads and proposes AHD, a training strategy that distributes safety capabilities across more heads, enhancing robustness against jailbreak attacks while preserving utility.
papers.conclusion: This work addresses concentrated safety vulnerabilities in LLMs by introducing RDSHA for identifying critical heads and proposing AHD to distribute safety, which improves resistance to jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are concentrated in a small subset of attention heads, as identified by RDSHA.
Ablating these critical attention heads significantly compromises model safety, increasing harmfulness rates.
Jailbreak attacks exploit this sparsity by selectively bypassing or suppressing safety-critical heads.
AHD distributes safety alignment across more attention heads, making models more robust to ablation and jailbreak attacks.
Models trained with AHD maintain overall utility without increasing over-refusal of benign queries.
papers.limitation: Reliance on a limited subset of the Alpaca dataset as a utility anchor during fine-tuning, preventing conclusive determination of utility drops.
future_direction: Access more diverse and comprehensive utility datasets for fine-tuning.
Explore alternative utility-preserving objectives and multi-task learning strategies.
papers.abstract: Current safety alignment for large language models(LLMs) continues to present vulnerabilities, given that adversarial prompting can effectively bypass their safety measures.Our investigation shows that these safety mechanisms predominantly depend on a limited subset of attention heads: removing or ablating these heads can severely compromise model safety. To identify and evaluate these safety-critical components, we introduce RDSHA, a targeted ablation method that leverages the model's refusal direction to pinpoint attention heads mostly responsible for safety behaviors. Further analysis shows that existing jailbreak attacks exploit this concentration by selectively bypassing or manipulating these critical attention heads. To address this issue, we propose AHD, a novel training strategy designed to promote the distributed encoding of safety-related behaviors across numerous attention heads. Experimental results demonstrate that AHD successfully distributes safety-related capabilities across more attention heads. Moreover, evaluations under several mainstream jailbreak attacks show that models trained with AHD exhibit considerably stronger safety robustness, while maintaining overall functional utility.

papers.title: Understanding Jailbreak Success: A Study of Latent Space Dynamics in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do different jailbreak types circumvent model safeguards, and do they operate via a similar internal mechanism? Specifically, can a jailbreak vector from one class mitigate jailbreaks from other classes, and is harmfulness suppression a common mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak vectors extracted from one class of jailbreaks can mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other, semantically dissimilar classes, suggesting a shared internal mechanism. Effective jailbreaks consistently reduce the model's perception of prompt harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: The transferability of jailbreak steering vectors suggests mitigation approaches may be generalizable, and harmfulness suppression is a common mechanism, offering insights for developing more robust countermeasures.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak types cluster in activation space based on semantic similarity.
Jailbreak steering vectors exhibit positive cosine similarity across different types.
Steering with a jailbreak vector (subtracting it) can prevent successful jailbreaks from its own and other classes.
Adding a jailbreak vector can induce jailbreaks, indicating the vectors capture what makes jailbreaks successful.
Successful jailbreaks reduce the cosine similarity between model activations and a harmfulness direction, though the degree of reduction does not clearly correlate with attack success rate.
papers.limitation:
Steering with jailbreak vectors occasionally reduces answer quality in the form of repetitions.
The significance of harmfulness reduction does not clearly map with the attack success rate of a jailbreak, indicating it might not be the only mechanism.
future_direction: Investigate other potential mechanisms beyond harmfulness suppression that could explain jailbreak success.
Explore the interaction of jailbreak types with a helpfulness feature direction.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are trained to refuse to answer harmful questions. However, emergent jailbreaking techniques can still elicit unsafe outputs, presenting an ongoing challenge for model alignment. To better understand how different jailbreak types circumvent safeguards, this paper analyses model activations on different jailbreak inputs. We find that it is possible to extract a jailbreak vector from a single class of jailbreaks that works to mitigate jailbreak effectiveness from other semantically-dissimilar classes. This may indicate that different kinds of effective jailbreaks operate via a similar internal mechanism. We investigate a potential common mechanism of harmfulness feature suppression, and find evidence that effective jailbreaks noticeably reduce a model's perception of prompt harmfulness. These findings offer actionable insights for developing more robust jailbreak countermeasures and lay the groundwork for a deeper, mechanistic understanding of jailbreak dynamics in language models.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time activation interventions at specific attention heads bypass safety alignments and steer LLMs towards harmful AI coordination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), a method that uses attention-head-level probing and intervention to steer LLM behavior, showing it can effectively induce misaligned AI coordination and outperforms layer-wise interventions and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: HSI is an effective method for steering LLM behavior, demonstrating that activations at specific attention heads encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviors and that current alignment techniques can be bypassed without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
HSI can bypass safety alignments and steer models towards harmful AI coordination.
HSI generalizes from binary choice to open-ended generation settings.
HSI is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning.
Only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions.
Applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack.
papers.limitation:
If intervention directions vary significantly between examples, calculating the mean across positive and negative labels may produce a direction that is ineffective for steering the model.
Sweeping over all attention heads could become computationally expensive for larger models with more attention heads.
future_direction: Further optimization of the technique to identify patterns and relevant heads without sweeping over all model components.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of models with more substantial differences in pre-training data, fine-tuning procedures, and architectural design.
Investigate alignment patterns within model activations and reasons for opposing directions in outlier examples to refine intervention methods.
papers.abstract: Robust alignment guardrails for large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly important with their widespread application. In contrast to previous studies, we demonstrate that inference-time activation interventions can bypass safety alignments and effectively steer model generations towards harmful AI coordination. Our method applies fine-grained interventions at specific attention heads, which we identify by probing each head in a simple binary choice task. We then show that interventions on these heads generalise to the open-ended generation setting, effectively circumventing safety guardrails. We demonstrate that intervening on a few attention heads is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning. We further show that only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions, which is an advantage over classical fine-tuning. We also demonstrate that applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack. Our results suggest that, at the attention head level, activations encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviours. Practically, the approach offers a straightforward methodology to steer large language model behaviour, which could be extended to diverse domains beyond safety, requiring fine-grained control over the model output. The code and datasets for this study can be found on https://github.com/PaulDrm/targeted_intervention.

papers.title: Revisiting Jailbreaking for Large Language Models: A Representation Engineering Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms that make Large Language Models vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks, and are these linked to specific activation patterns in their representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'safety patterns' in LLMs' representation space that are crucial for self-safeguarding against malicious queries, and shows these patterns can be extracted and manipulated to control jailbreak vulnerability.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a new interpretation of jailbreaking through safety patterns, offering insights for attack and defense strategies, and raises concerns about the misuse of open-source LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Safety patterns can be extracted from LLMs using only a few contrastive query pairs.
Weakening safety patterns significantly reduces LLMs' self-safeguard capability, leading to successful jailbreaks.
Strengthening safety patterns enhances defense against stealthy jailbreak prompts.
Manipulating safety patterns has minimal impact on LLMs' general abilities and output quality.
Visualization analysis confirms that safety patterns affect the embedding distribution of malicious and benign inputs.
papers.limitation:
The findings are based on white-box settings, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Preventing misuse of safety pattern manipulation is a critical challenge.
future_direction: Exploring effective techniques such as Reverse Engineering based on the concept of safety patterns.
Developing comprehensive safeguarding strategies to ensure the safer use of LLMs, particularly in open-source models.
papers.abstract: The recent surge in jailbreaking attacks has revealed significant vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) when exposed to malicious inputs. While various defense strategies have been proposed to mitigate these threats, there has been limited research into the underlying mechanisms that make LLMs vulnerable to such attacks. In this study, we suggest that the self-safeguarding capability of LLMs is linked to specific activity patterns within their representation space. Although these patterns have little impact on the semantic content of the generated text, they play a crucial role in shaping LLM behavior under jailbreaking attacks. Our findings demonstrate that these patterns can be detected with just a few pairs of contrastive queries. Extensive experimentation shows that the robustness of LLMs against jailbreaking can be manipulated by weakening or strengthening these patterns. Further visual analysis provides additional evidence for our conclusions, providing new insights into the jailbreaking phenomenon. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the potential misuse of open-source LLMs within the community.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
