The method achieves competitive or improved performance compared to state-of-the-art parameter-efficient cross-lingual transfer methods like Sparse Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Target Language-Ready (TLR) adapters.
Scaling factors for language vectors significantly impact performance, and optimal values vary across tasks and languages.
Imposing sparsity on language vectors generally degrades performance, indicating that a more refined approach is needed for sparsity to be beneficial in this context.
The task analogy variant (-SRC +TGT) underperforms compared to simply adding the target language vector, suggesting that source language knowledge is valuable and should not be suppressed.
papers.limitation:
The work is a short paper with page constraints, limiting the extent and depth of experiments and analysis.
All results are based on a single run due to the large number of languages and methods, though averaging over many targets and replication with two models enhances confidence.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to different model types (e.g., encoder-decoder models) and in few-shot cross-lingual transfer scenarios.
Develop more nuanced, per-parameter weighting methods for the vectors, potentially using Fisher information.
Investigate more refined sparsity approaches for language vectors, possibly involving re-training or sophisticated parameter selection.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer has recently been tackled through modular, parameter-efficient finetuning methods which allow arbitrary combinations of language and task modules for transfer of any task to any language.Concurrently, task arithmetic has emerged as a powerful and modular tool for editing pretrained models using multiple full fine-tunings.In this work, we connect the paradigms of task arithmetic and crosslingual transfer, demonstrating that modularity for cross-lingual transfer can be achieved even with full model fine-tuning.Our approach displays strong performance on a range of multilingual benchmarks encompassing both highresource and low-resource languages.

papers.title: There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction
papers.research_question: How different are the refusal directions when computed for different types of refusal behavior beyond safety, and how do these directions get expressed in the latent space such that they facilitate various styles of refusal under a similar intervention mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal behavior in LLMs is mediated by multiple geometrically distinct activation-space directions, but linear steering along any refusal-related direction acts as a one-dimensional control knob for refusal, with differences primarily in refusal style. Sparse autoencoders reveal a structured internal representation with a shared core of refusal latents and a long tail of style-specific latents.
papers.conclusion: The internal structure of refusal is rich and structured, but linear control flattens this complexity, highlighting the limits of linear interpretability for aligned model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Different refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space.
Linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob.
The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses (style).
Sparse autoencoders uncover a structured internal representation: a small reusable core of shared refusal latents supplemented by a long tail of style- and domain-specific latents.
Linear interventions collapse over this structure, flattening mechanistic differences into uniform behavioral control.
papers.limitation:
The techniques could be misused to suppress refusal behavior and facilitate the generation of harmful content.
Linear steering collapses a rich internal refusal structure into a coarse behavioral knob, underscoring that such interventions are not suitable as principled safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Prior work argues that refusal in large language models is mediated by a single activation-space direction, enabling effective steering and ablation. We show that this account is incomplete. Across eleven categories of refusal and non-compliance, including safety, incomplete or unsupported requests, anthropomorphization, and over-refusal, we find that these refusal behaviors correspond to geometrically distinct directions in activation space. Yet despite this diversity, linear steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal to over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob. The primary effect of different directions is not whether the model refuses, but how it refuses.

papers.title: Interpretation Meets Safety: A Survey on Interpretation Methods and Tools for Improving LLM Safety
papers.core_contribution: This survey bridges the gap between LLM interpretation and safety, introducing a unified framework that connects safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancements they inform, and the tools that operationalize them.
papers.conclusion: This timely survey helps researchers and practitioners navigate key advancements for safer, more interpretable LLMs and outlines open challenges for future work.
papers.key_findings:
This is the first survey to bridge LLM interpretation and safety, providing a unified framework for summarizing safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancement strategies they inform, and the practical tools that operationalize them.
It introduces a novel taxonomy of LLM interpretation methods organized by LLM workflow stages: training process, input prompts, inference, and generation for self-reasoning.
The taxonomy connects interpretation methods to six safety enhancement strategies and four tool types, summarizing nearly 70 works at their intersections.
The survey distills open problems and challenges to guide future NLP research and raise awareness of unresolved safety issues.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) see wider real-world use, understanding and mitigating their unsafe behaviors is critical. Interpretation techniques can reveal causes of unsafe outputs and guide safety, but such connections with safety are often overlooked in prior surveys. We present the first survey that bridges this gap, introducing a unified framework that connects safety-focused interpretation methods, the safety enhancements they inform, and the tools that operationalize them. Our novel taxonomy, organized by LLM workflow stages, summarizes nearly 70 works at their intersections. We conclude with open challenges and future directions. This timely survey helps researchers and practitioners navigate key advancements for safer, more interpretable LLMs.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Security Tensors as a Cross-Modal Bridge: Extending Text-Aligned Safety to Vision in LVLM
papers.research_question: How can we extend the text-aligned safety mechanisms of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to the visual modality to protect against harmful image inputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces security tensors, trainable input vectors applied during inference, to transfer textual safety alignment to visual processing in LVLMs without modifying the model's parameters.
papers.conclusion: Security tensors effectively extend text-aligned safety mechanisms to the visual modality, acting as a cross-modal bridge to protect LVLMs from harmful image inputs.
papers.key_findings:
Security tensors (both visual and textual) significantly improve the harmless rate on harmful visual inputs while maintaining benign performance.
Security tensors generalize to unseen harmful categories, indicating they do not simply memorize visual patterns.
The Text Contrast Benign (TCB) set is crucial to prevent the security tensors from overfitting to textual patterns.
Security tensors activate the language module's safety layers (layers 9-20 in LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision) for harmful visual inputs, bridging the cross-modal safety gap.
papers.abstract: Large visual-language models (LVLMs) integrate aligned large language models (LLMs) with visual modules to process multimodal inputs. However, the safety mechanisms developed for text-based LLMs do not naturally extend to visual modalities, leaving LVLMs vulnerable to harmful image inputs. To address this cross-modal safety gap, we introduce security tensors - trainable input vectors applied during inference through either the textual or visual modality. These tensors transfer textual safety alignment to visual processing without modifying the model's parameters. They are optimized using a curated dataset containing (i) malicious image-text pairs requiring rejection, (ii) contrastive benign pairs with text structurally similar to malicious queries, with the purpose of being contrastive examples to guide visual reliance, and (iii) general benign samples preserving model functionality. Experimental results demonstrate that both textual and visual security tensors significantly enhance LVLMs' ability to reject diverse harmful visual inputs while maintaining near-identical performance on benign tasks. Further internal analysis towards hidden-layer representations reveals that security tensors successfully activate the language module's textual "safety layers" in visual inputs, thereby effectively extending text-based safety to the visual modality.

papers.title: PIP: Detecting Adversarial Examples in Large Vision-Language Models via Attention Patterns of Irrelevant Probe Questions
papers.research_question: How can adversarial examples in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be detected using attention patterns from irrelevant probe questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PIP, a simple method that uses the attention patterns of a randomly selected irrelevant probe question (e.g., 'Is there a clock?') to distinguish adversarial examples from clean examples in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: PIP is a simple and effective method for detecting adversarial examples in LVLMs, achieving high recall and low false alarms, which can enhance the security and robustness of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit regular attention patterns for clean images when presented with yes/no probe questions.
The attention patterns of clean and adversarial examples in response to the same irrelevant probe question are clearly distinguishable and linearly separable.
PIP, coupled with a simple SVM classifier, achieves high recall (>98%) and precision (>90%) for detecting adversarial examples, even under black-box attacks and across different datasets.
The method generalizes across different attack methods (PGD, C&W), attack parameters, and various LVLM architectures.
Using multiple probe questions and SVMs can alleviate the high false alarm rate issue while maintaining high recall.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated their powerful multimodal capabilities. However, they also face serious safety problems, as adversaries can induce robustness issues in LVLMs through the use of well-designed adversarial examples. Therefore, LVLMs are in urgent need of detection tools for adversarial examples to prevent incorrect responses. In this work, we first discover that LVLMs exhibit regular attention patterns for clean images when presented with probe questions. We propose an unconventional method named PIP, which utilizes the attention patterns of one randomly selected irrelevant probe question (e.g., "Is there a clock''') to distinguish adversarial examples from clean examples. Regardless of the image to be tested and its corresponding question, PIP only needs to perform one additional inference of the image to be tested and the probe question, and then achieves successful detection of adversarial examples. Even under black-box attacks and open dataset scenarios, our PIP, coupled with a simple SVM, still achieves more than 98% recall and a precision of over 90%. Our PIP is the first attempt to detect adversarial attacks on LVLMs via simple irrelevant probe questions, shedding light on deeper understanding and introspection within LVLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/btzyd/pip.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: The Straight and Narrow: Do LLMs Possess an Internal Moral Path?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess an internal moral path, or are they merely capturing superficial linguistic artifacts? The paper investigates the internal moral representations of LLMs and how to manipulate them for safety.
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps Moral Foundations Theory onto the latent space of LLMs, confirming linearly separable moral representations, and introduces Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) to dynamically steer these representations for safety, effectively balancing the safety-helpfulness trade-off.
papers.conclusion: The work bridges the gap between superficial behavioral guardrails and intrinsic alignment by mapping and manipulating moral representations within LLMs, demonstrating that activation engineering can serve as a robust intrinsic defense mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode linearly separable moral representations in their middle layers, forming a shared yet distinct moral subspace across English and Chinese.
Steerable Moral Vectors can be extracted and causally modulate the model's internal state and behavioral output, shifting responses between 'Virtue' and 'Vice'.
Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF) synergizes probe detection with vector injection, reducing jailbreak success rates on HarmBench while minimizing incorrect refusals on XSTest.
Cross-lingual analysis reveals 'Asymmetric Feature Coverage' where some moral concepts (e.g., Care, Loyalty-Vice) are more richly encoded in Chinese, while others (e.g., Sanctity-Virtue, Authority-Virtue) are more robust in English.
Moral Vector injection reveals implicit correlations between foundations, such as Fairness and Loyalty amplifying Authority-virtue, and identifies Sanctity-vice as a 'universal negative pole'.
papers.limitation:
The cultural and theoretical scope is limited to English and Chinese and grounded solely in Moral Foundations Theory, potentially overlooking other ethical frameworks and low-resource cultures.
The Moral Virtue-Vice dataset was generated by an LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) without large-scale human annotation, potentially reflecting the generator's biases.
Validation was primarily on the Llama-3.1 family; generalizability to other architectures requires further study.
future_direction: Extending the framework to diverse model architectures.
Expanding the cross-lingual analysis to capture a broader spectrum of global cultural morality.
Incorporating ethical frameworks beyond Moral Foundations Theory.
papers.abstract: Enhancing the moral alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in AI safety. Current alignment techniques often act as superficial guardrails, leaving the intrinsic moral representations of LLMs largely untouched. In this paper, we bridge this gap by leveraging Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) to map and manipulate the fine-grained moral landscape of LLMs. Through cross-lingual linear probing, we validate the shared nature of moral representations in middle layers and uncover a shared yet different moral subspace between English and Chinese. Building upon this, we extract steerable Moral Vectors and successfully validate their efficacy at both internal and behavioral levels. Leveraging the high generalizability of morality, we propose Adaptive Moral Fusion (AMF), a dynamic inference-time intervention that synergizes probe detection with vector injection to tackle the safety-helpfulness trade-off. Empirical results confirm that our approach acts as a targeted intrinsic defense, effectively reducing incorrect refusals on benign queries while minimizing jailbreak success rates compared to standard baselines.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in overlapping subsets of neurons across languages, with the extent of overlap varying by category, language proximity, and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, which may underpin their ability to generalize across languages and facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
There is significant cross-lingual overlap of neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
The overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and tends to be lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Neuron subsets are shared more between languages in the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with the amount of pre-training data for a language.
Overlap decreases in larger model architectures (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
future_direction: Artificially encouraging tighter neuron overlap might facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: Karolina Stanczak, Edoardo Ponti, Lucas Torroba Hennigen, Ryan Cotterell, Isabelle Augenstein. Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2022.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: SteeringSafety: A Systematic Safety Evaluation Framework of Representation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do representation steering methods affect various safety perspectives, and what are the entanglement patterns when steering for specific safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEERINGSAFETY, a framework for systematic evaluation of representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives, revealing that steering effectiveness and entanglement depend on method-model-perspective pairings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation steering methods exhibit complex entanglement patterns, and a holistic safety evaluation is necessary to understand and mitigate unintended side effects.
papers.key_findings:
DIM and ACE are generally effective for harmfulness and bias steering, while PCA and LAT are promising for hallucination in certain models.
Entanglement is model-dependent but consistently highest for social behaviors and normative judgment, while reasoning remains robust.
Different steering methods targeting the same behavior can create steering vectors entangling distinct perspectives.
Conditional steering enables better effectiveness-entanglement tradeoffs for most perspectives but cannot completely mitigate entanglement.
Jailbreaking doesn't necessarily increase toxicity, hallucination steering causes opposing political shifts across models, and improving one bias type can degrade another.
papers.limitation:
Focus on English-language datasets and instruction-tuned models
Steering is implemented as static vectors applied at fixed model locations, overlooking more adaptive methods
Results are reported in aggregate, potentially obscuring nuanced shifts within behavioral subtypes
future_direction: Expand framework to incorporate weight modifications and other representation engineering approaches
Investigate reasoning models and steering from tokens other than final post-instruction tokens
Generalize findings to other model deployment settings, such as agentic safety and security
papers.abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a systematic framework for evaluating representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives spanning 17 datasets. While prior work highlights general capabilities of representation steering, we systematically explore safety perspectives including bias, harmfulness, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. Our framework provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements like conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B reveal that strong steering performance depends critically on pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. DIM shows consistent effectiveness, but all methods exhibit substantial entanglement: social behaviors show highest vulnerability (reaching degradation as high as 76%), jailbreaking often compromises normative judgment, and hallucination steering unpredictably shifts political views. Our findings underscore the critical need for holistic safety evaluations.

papers.title: The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence
papers.research_question: How is refusal behavior mediated in large language models? Is it controlled by a single direction or by more complex geometric structures such as multiple independent directions and concept cones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a gradient-based representation engineering method (RDO) to identify refusal directions, discovers multi-dimensional refusal cones, and proposes representational independence to characterize independent directions.
papers.conclusion: The work advances understanding of refusal mechanisms in LLMs through gradient-based representation engineering, showing refusal is governed by high-dimensional cones and multiple independent directions, providing a framework for analyzing representational interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-based Refusal Direction Optimization (RDO) yields more effective refusal directions with fewer side effects compared to difference-in-means (DIM) baselines.
Refusal behavior is mediated by multi-dimensional polyhedral cones (concept cones) in activation space, not a single linear direction.
Orthogonality does not guarantee independence under intervention; representational independence accounts for linear and non-linear dependencies.
Multiple representationally independent refusal directions exist, indicating distinct underlying mechanisms.
These independent directions can be accessed via input manipulations (e.g., adversarial suffixes) and compositionally ablated to improve jailbreak success.
papers.limitation:
The refusal directions are optimized on the same targets, which may limit their ability to capture fully distinct mechanisms.
Cannot rule out the possibility of other yet-undiscovered regions in the model that mediate refusal.
future_direction: Extending the method to incorporate diverse targets or leveraging reinforcement learning with a judge-based reward function to identify additional independent mechanisms.
Applying the gradient-based representation engineering approach to identify various concepts beyond refusal by changing optimization targets.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: From Defender to Devil? Unintended Risk Interactions Induced by LLM Defenses
papers.research_question: How do defenses targeting one risk (safety, fairness, privacy) in LLMs affect other risks, and what are the internal mechanisms driving these unintended interactions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a cross-risk evaluation paradigm (CrossRiskEval) and demonstrates that defenses targeting a single risk in LLMs often induce measurable, asymmetric side effects on other risks, which originate from conflict-entangled neurons in the model's internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Single-risk evaluation is insufficient; holistic and interaction-aware assessment is necessary for designing and deploying balanced, robust LLM defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Defenses targeting a single risk (safety, fairness, privacy) often cause measurable effects on other risks, with effects varying in direction and magnitude across models, tasks, and defense strategies.
Cross-risk interactions are often asymmetric; for example, fairness defenses can significantly increase privacy risks, while privacy defenses may have minimal or even positive effects on fairness.
Safety defenses can suppress direct responses to sensitive queries but paradoxically amplify indirect privacy leakage or biased outputs.
Conflict-entangled neurons—shared internal representations that contribute in opposite ways to different risks—are identified as the internal origin of these unintended cross-risk interactions.
The findings reveal the limits of single-risk evaluation and highlight the need for holistic, interaction-aware assessment when designing and deploying LLM defenses.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation, while broad, is not exhaustive due to the rapid evolution of models and defenses.
The risk taxonomy is limited to safety, fairness, and privacy, though the framework can be extended to other dimensions.
The focus is on endogenous defenses (model weights/training), excluding system-level filters.
future_direction: Extend the risk taxonomy to incorporate additional risk dimensions (e.g., hallucination).
Incorporate neuron-aware strategies into defense design to mitigate cross-risk conflicts.
Explore the interplay between endogenous defenses and exogenous system-level filters.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance across various applications, but their deployment in real-world settings faces several risks, including jailbreak attacks and privacy leaks. To mitigate these risks, numerous defense strategies have been proposed. However, most existing studies assess these defenses in isolation and ignore their effects on other risk dimensions. In this work, we introduce a new cross-risk evaluation paradigm and take the first step in investigating unintended interactions among defenses in LLMs. Specifically, we focus on the interplay between safety, fairness, and privacy. To this end, we propose CrossRiskEval, a framework that systematically characterizes how a defense designed for one risk (e.g., safety) affects others (e.g., fairness or privacy). We conduct extensive empirical studies and mechanistic analyses on 14 LLMs with deployed defenses, covering 12 defense strategies. Our results show that defenses targeting a single risk often cause measurable effects on other risks. These effects vary in direction and magnitude across a range of factors (e.g., models, tasks, and defense strategies), and are often asymmetric across risk pairs. Furthermore, our mechanistic analysis shows that these interactions are not random: they arise from conflict-entangled neurons, which are shared internal representations that contribute in opposite ways to different risks. Adjusting one risk therefore perturbs these representations and leads to systematic changes in non-target risks. These findings reveal the limits of single-risk evaluation and highlight the need for holistic and interaction-aware assessment when designing and deploying LLM defenses.

papers.title: White Noise Analysis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the inherent biases of deep neural networks and how can we understand and visualize them using methods from computational neuroscience (classification images and spike triggered analysis)?
papers.core_contribution: White noise analysis (using classification images and spike triggered averaging) can reveal inherent biases in neural networks, visualize filters, and be used for adversarial attack and defense.
papers.conclusion: White noise analysis is effective for understanding and interpreting neural networks, demonstrating successful cross-fertilization between neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Classification images derived from white noise resemble target classes and can be used for classification above chance level.
Classification images can be used to attack black-box classifiers by adding bias maps to inputs.
Classification images can detect adversarial patch attacks by revealing perturbed regions.
Spike triggered averaging can visualize filters in CNNs, showing oriented edges similar to those learned from real data.
Micro-stimulation of neurons in different layers can bias network decisions, producing psychometric curves similar to biological systems.
papers.limitation:
Requires a large number of trials (sample complexity) to compute classification images.
Classification images over natural scene datasets may not resemble sharp object instances.
future_direction: Apply the tools to more complex CNN architectures (e.g., ResNet, InceptionNet) and other models (e.g., CapsuleNets, GANs).
Use classification images to detect and defend against other types of adversarial attacks.
Apply classification images and spike triggered analysis to other computer vision tasks (e.g., object detection, segmentation).
papers.abstract: A white noise analysis of modern deep neural networks is presented to unveil their biases at the whole network level or the single neuron level. Our analysis is based on two popular and related methods in psychophysics and neurophysiology namely classification images and spike triggered analysis. These methods have been widely used to understand the underlying mechanisms of sensory systems in humans and monkeys. We leverage them to investigate the inherent biases of deep neural networks and to obtain a first-order approximation of their functionality. We emphasize on CNNs since they are currently the state of the art methods in computer vision and are a decent model of human visual processing. In addition, we study multi-layer perceptrons, logistic regression, and recurrent neural networks. Experiments over four classic datasets, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, show that the computed bias maps resemble the target classes and when used for classification lead to an over twofold performance than the chance level. Further, we show that classification images can be used to attack a black-box classifier and to detect adversarial patch attacks. Finally, we utilize spike triggered averaging to derive the filters of CNNs and explore how the behavior of a network changes when neurons in different layers are modulated. Our effort illustrates a successful example of borrowing from neurosciences to study ANNs and highlights the importance of cross-fertilization and synergy across machine learning, deep learning, and computational neuroscience.

papers.title: A safety realignment framework via subspace-oriented model fusion for large language models
papers.research_question: How to realign fine-tuned large language models to restore safety without compromising downstream task performance, for both single and multiple task-specific models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a safety realignment framework via subspace-oriented model fusion (SOMF) that restores safety in fine-tuned LLMs by identifying and reusing safety-critical subspaces, without significant performance loss on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed SOMF framework provides an effective method for safety realignment of LLMs, balancing safety restoration and utility preservation for both single and multiple task-specific models.
papers.key_findings:
SOMF effectively realigns single task-specific models to improve safety while preserving downstream task performance.
SOMF successfully realigns multiple task-specific models during fusion, maintaining safety in the fused model.
The method identifies safety-critical regions in task vectors via subspace masking techniques.
SOMF demonstrates robust safety improvements across various harmful topics and against different attack prompts.
The realignment framework works with both full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) strategies.
papers.abstract: The current safeguard mechanisms for large language models (LLMs) are indeed susceptible to jailbreak attacks, making them inherently fragile. Even the process of fine-tuning on apparently benign data for downstream tasks can jeopardize safety. One potential solution is to conduct safety fine-tuning subsequent to downstream fine-tuning. However, there's a risk of catastrophic forgetting during safety fine-tuning, where LLMs may regain safety measures but lose the task-specific knowledge acquired during downstream fine-tuning. In this paper, we introduce a safety realignment framework through subspace-oriented model fusion (SOMF), aiming to combine the safeguard capabilities of initially aligned model and the current fine-tuned model into a realigned model. Our approach begins by disentangling all task vectors from the weights of each fine-tuned model. We then identify safety-related regions within these vectors by subspace masking techniques. Finally, we explore the fusion of the initial safely aligned LLM with all task vectors based on the identified safety subspace. We validate that our safety realignment framework satisfies the safety requirements of a single fine-tuned model as well as multiple models during their fusion. Our findings confirm that SOMF preserves safety without notably compromising performance on downstream tasks, including instruction following in Chinese, English, and Hindi, as well as problem-solving capabilities in Code and Math.

papers.title: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models?: Geometry might be the answer
papers.research_question: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models? The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain their effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, suggesting that triggers act as embedding vectors approximating the semantic meaning of adversarial text.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a geometric perspective that potentially explains universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, with evidence that triggers approximate semantic information in embedding space, aiming to shed light on failure modes and enable mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Universal adversarial triggers are effective on large language models and can transfer across models, as shown with GPT-2, DistilBERT, and OPT-350M.
Self-attention probing indicates that the last token in triggers is highly attended to, suggesting positional importance.
Perturbing trigger tokens shows that semantic meaning and token position affect the adversarial output, with deletions reducing effectiveness.
Dimensionality reduction using UMAP reveals that triggers cluster with adversarial text in embedding space, supporting the geometric hypothesis.
The geometric perspective suggests that universal adversarial triggers behave like embedding vectors that approximate the semantic region of their adversarial training text.
papers.limitation:
The usage of dimensionality reduction could be providing an incomplete picture.
The analysis on trigger perturbations is performed on a single trigger and may not be generalizable.
future_direction: Expanding experimentation to additional techniques such as studying layer-wise distances, visualizing hidden representations evolution, and analyzing KL divergence.
Understanding the transferability of universal attacks across different models.
papers.abstract: Transformer based large language models with emergent capabilities are becoming increasingly ubiquitous in society. However, the task of understanding and interpreting their internal workings, in the context of adversarial attacks, remains largely unsolved. Gradient-based universal adversarial attacks have been shown to be highly effective on large language models and potentially dangerous due to their input-agnostic nature. This work presents a novel geometric perspective explaining universal adversarial attacks on large language models. By attacking the 117M parameter GPT-2 model, we find evidence indicating that universal adversarial triggers could be embedding vectors which merely approximate the semantic information in their adversarial training region. This hypothesis is supported by white-box model analysis comprising dimensionality reduction and similarity measurement of hidden representations. We believe this new geometric perspective on the underlying mechanism driving universal attacks could help us gain deeper insight into the internal workings and failure modes of LLMs, thus enabling their mitigation.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Safety Arithmetic: A Framework for Test-time Safety Alignment of Language Models by Steering Parameters and Activations
papers.research_question: Can an existing approach handle all three scenarios (base models, supervised fine-tuned models, and edited models) efficiently for safety alignment while preserving model general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAFETY ARITHMETIC, a training-free framework for test-time safety alignment of language models across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited models by removing harmful directions from parameters and steering activations toward safe responses.
papers.conclusion: SAFETY ARITHMETIC effectively improves safety measures, mitigates over-safety, and preserves utility across base, supervised fine-tuned, and edited language models, outperforming existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAFETY ARITHMETIC significantly reduces attack success rates (ASR) across multiple safety datasets (e.g., AdvBench, DangerousQA) for base, fine-tuned, and edited models.
The framework maintains model utility on standard benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) and reduces over-safety (lower refusal rates on benign queries).
The Harm Direction Removal (HDR) stage using top-k parameter selection and the Safety Alignment (Safe-Align) stage using an in-context safety vector (ICV) are both effective components.
The method outperforms baselines like HDR with TIES, HDR with Task Vector, and Safe-Align with ICV alone.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models with up to 7 billion parameters, not representing larger models (>7B).
In HDR, selecting the top k parameters in the harm vector is crucial; changing too many parameters may impair the model's general abilities.
In Safe-Align, determining the fraction of the ICV vector to add to token representations during inference is important.
future_direction: Optimize hyperparameters, such as the scaling factor for harm vector application and the strength of in-context vectors, to enhance the framework's precision, robustness, and reliability across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Ensuring the safe alignment of large language models (LLMs) with human values is critical as they become integral to applications like translation and question answering. Current alignment methods struggle with dynamic user intentions and complex objectives, making models vulnerable to generating harmful content. We propose Safety Arithmetic, a training-free framework enhancing LLM safety across different scenarios: Base models, Supervised fine-tuned models (SFT), and Edited models. Safety Arithmetic involves Harm Direction Removal to avoid harmful content and Safety Alignment to promote safe responses. Additionally, we present NoIntentEdit, a dataset highlighting edit instances that could compromise model safety if used unintentionally. Our experiments show that Safety Arithmetic significantly improves safety measures, reduces over-safety, and maintains model utility, outperforming existing methods in ensuring safe content generation.

papers.title: Making Harmful Behaviors Unlearnable for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a controllable fine-tuning framework using 'security vectors' (additional parameters) to make harmful behaviors unlearnable during training, preventing LLMs from learning from harmful data while preserving their ability to learn other tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework with security vectors effectively prevents LLMs from learning harmful behaviors during fine-tuning, reducing security risks and enabling safer model customization.
papers.key_findings:
Security vectors trained on 100 harmful samples can prevent an LLM from learning harmful behaviors from 1000 harmful examples.
The method prevents learning from both explicit and implicit harmful data, maintaining safety levels comparable to the original aligned model.
Fine-tuning with security vectors does not impair the model's ability to learn new, benign tasks (e.g., ProfileQA).
The approach is robust across different training epochs and learning rates, except when the fine-tuning learning rate is much higher than that used to generate the security vectors.
Security vectors can be deactivated during inference, restoring the model's normal, safe behavior.
papers.limitation:
The security vectors may lose effectiveness if the fine-tuning learning rate is significantly higher (e.g., 5e-3) than the rate used to generate them (1e-3).
Excessive training epochs on harmful data may impair the model's reasoning ability (e.g., on GSM), though the cause is not fully determined.
future_direction: Design experiments to ascertain the cause of the drop in reasoning ability (GSM) when fine-tuning on harmful data.
Investigate the robust instruction-following capability observed when fine-tuning with security vectors over many epochs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose AI assistants in various domains. To meet the requirements of different applications, LLMs are often customized by further fine-tuning. However, the powerful learning ability of LLMs not only enables them to acquire new tasks but also makes them susceptible to learning undesired behaviors. For example, even safety-aligned LLMs can be easily fine-tuned into harmful assistants as the fine-tuning data often contains implicit or explicit harmful content. Can we train LLMs on harmful data without learning harmful behaviors? This paper proposes a controllable training framework that makes harmful behaviors unlearnable during the fine-tuning process. Specifically, we introduce ``security vectors'', a few new parameters that can be separated from the LLM, to ensure LLM's responses are consistent with the harmful behavior. Security vectors are activated during fine-tuning, the consistent behavior makes LLM believe that such behavior has already been learned, there is no need to further optimize for harmful data. During inference, we can deactivate security vectors to restore the LLM's normal behavior. The experimental results show that the security vectors generated by 100 harmful samples are enough to prevent LLM from learning 1000 harmful samples, while preserving the ability to learn other useful information.

papers.title: SafeInfer: Context Adaptive Decoding Time Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to ensure safety in language models at decoding time, addressing fragile safety mechanisms and safety compromise after model editing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAFE INFER, a two-phase decoding-time safety alignment method that adapts to context via safety amplification and guided decoding, maintaining model utility.
papers.conclusion: SAFE INFER is a valuable framework for enhancing safety and reliability of language models in various applications through adaptive decoding-time alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAFE INFER consistently achieves the lowest attack success rates across multiple datasets and models.
The method preserves the utility of the base models on standard benchmarks.
SAFE INFER is effective against various jailbreak attacks.
It also reduces harm in edited models.
The method balances low ASR and low over-safety at an optimal hyperparameter setting.
papers.abstract: Language models aligned for safety often exhibit fragile and imbalanced mechanisms, increasing the chances of producing unsafe content. In addition, editing techniques to incorporate new knowledge can further compromise safety. To tackle these issues, we propose SafeInfer, a context-adaptive, decoding-time safety alignment strategy for generating safe responses to user queries. safeInfer involves two phases: the 'safety amplification' phase, which uses safe demonstration examples to adjust the model’s hidden states and increase the likelihood of safer outputs, and the 'safety-guided decoding' phase, which influences token selection based on safety-optimized distributions to ensure the generated content adheres to ethical guidelines. Further, we introduce HarmEval, a novel benchmark for comprehensive safety evaluations, designed to address potential misuse scenarios in line with the policies of leading AI technology companies.

papers.title: Understanding Refusal in Language Models with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How is refusal encoded in the latent space of LLMs, and how do adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using sparse autoencoders to identify and causally validate refusal-related features in LLMs, revealing that harm and refusal are separately encoded and that adversarial jailbreaks suppress refusal features.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can identify causal refusal features, revealing the mediation of refusal by harmful features and the suppression mechanism of adversarial jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode harm and refusal as separate feature sets, with harmful features exhibiting a causal effect on refusal features.
Adversarial jailbreaks operate by suppressing specific refusal-related features.
The identified refusal features significantly improve classification on out-of-distribution adversarial examples.
The proposed CosSim+AP method identifies a minimal set of causal features for refusal behavior.
There is a conditional relationship where harmful features upstream trigger refusal features downstream.
papers.limitation:
The small K* may omit additional features relevant to harm and refusal.
The reliance on the refusal direction may not generalize to challenging instructions.
SAEs were trained on base models, not chat models, which may affect interpretability.
future_direction: Training SAEs on chat-model activations to improve feature interpretability and relevance.
papers.abstract: Refusal is a key safety behavior in aligned language models, yet the internal mechanisms driving refusals remain opaque. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study of refusal in instruction-tuned LLMs using sparse autoencoders to identify latent features that causally mediate refusal behaviors. We apply our method to two open-source chat models and intervene on refusal-related features to assess their influence on generation, validating their behavioral impact across multiple harmful datasets. This enables a fine-grained inspection of how refusal manifests at the activation level and addresses key research questions such as investigating upstream-downstream latent relationship and understanding the mechanisms of adversarial jailbreaking techniques. We also establish the usefulness of refusal features in enhancing generalization for linear probes to out-of-distribution adversarial samples in classification tasks. We open source our code in https://github.com/wj210/refusal_sae.

papers.title: How Jailbreak Defenses Work and Ensemble? A Mechanistic Investigation
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak defenses work in terms of safety shift and harmfulness discrimination, and how can they be ensembled to balance safety and helpfulness?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies two core mechanisms in jailbreak defenses (safety shift and harmfulness discrimination) and proposes inter-mechanism and intra-mechanism ensemble strategies to improve safety or balance it with helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed ensemble defense strategies, based on the identified safety shift and harmfulness discrimination mechanisms, effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness in multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Safety shift defenses increase refusal probabilities for both harmful and benign queries, improving safety but risking over-defense and reduced helpfulness.
Harmfulness discrimination defenses improve the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign queries, mitigating over-defense.
Inter-mechanism ensembles (combining methods with the same mechanism) amplify a single defense mechanism, while intra-mechanism ensembles (combining safety shift and harmfulness discrimination methods) achieve a better trade-off.
Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, with individual methods showing limited success rates, but ensemble strategies can improve performance.
Fine-tuning with safety-focused datasets (e.g., SPA-VL) can improve safety, but dataset choice (e.g., VLGuard) can lead to over-defense, which can be mitigated by adding general instruction data.
papers.limitation: Multimodal jailbreak defense is challenging, and all individual defense methods still exhibit limited defense success rates.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks, where harmful prompts bypass generative models' built-in safety, raise serious concerns about model vulnerability. While many defense methods have been proposed, the trade-offs between safety and helpfulness, and their application to Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), are not well understood. This paper systematically examines jailbreak defenses by reframing the standard generation task as a binary classification problem to assess model refusal tendencies for both harmful and benign queries. We identify two key defense mechanisms: safety shift, which increases refusal rates across all queries, and harmfulness discrimination, which improves the model's ability to distinguish between harmful and benign inputs. Using these mechanisms, we develop two ensemble defense strategies-inter-mechanism ensembles and intra-mechanism ensembles-to balance safety and helpfulness. Experiments on the MM-SafetyBench and MOSSBench datasets with LLaVA-1.5 models show that these strategies effectively improve model safety or optimize the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

papers.title: Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, they pose potential safety concerns, such as the ``jailbreak'' problem, wherein malicious instructions can manipulate LLMs to exhibit undesirable behavior. Although several preventive measures have been developed to mitigate the potential risks associated with LLMs, they have primarily focused on English. In this study, we reveal the presence of multilingual jailbreak challenges within LLMs and consider two potential risky scenarios: unintentional and intentional. The unintentional scenario involves users querying LLMs using non-English prompts and inadvertently bypassing the safety mechanisms, while the intentional scenario concerns malicious users combining malicious instructions with multilingual prompts to deliberately attack LLMs. The experimental results reveal that in the unintentional scenario, the rate of unsafe content increases as the availability of languages decreases. Specifically, low-resource languages exhibit about three times the likelihood of encountering harmful content compared to high-resource languages, with both ChatGPT and GPT-4. In the intentional scenario, multilingual prompts can exacerbate the negative impact of malicious instructions, with astonishingly high rates of unsafe output: 80.92\% for ChatGPT and 40.71\% for GPT-4. To handle such a challenge in the multilingual context, we propose a novel \textsc{Self-Defense} framework that automatically generates multilingual training data for safety fine-tuning. Experimental results show that ChatGPT fine-tuned with such data can achieve a substantial reduction in unsafe content generation. Data is available at \url{https://github.com/DAMO-NLP-SG/multilingual-safety-for-LLMs}.

papers.title: Safe2Harm: Semantic Isomorphism Attacks for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance across various tasks, but their security vulnerabilities can be exploited by attackers to generate harmful content, causing adverse impacts across various societal domains. Most existing jailbreak methods revolve around Prompt Engineering or adversarial optimization, yet we identify a previously overlooked phenomenon: many harmful scenarios are highly consistent with legitimate ones in terms of underlying principles. Based on this finding, this paper proposes the Safe2Harm Semantic Isomorphism Attack method, which achieves efficient jailbreaking through four stages: first, rewrite the harmful question into a semantically safe question with similar underlying principles; second, extract the thematic mapping relationship between the two; third, let the LLM generate a detailed response targeting the safe question; finally, reversely rewrite the safe response based on the thematic mapping relationship to obtain harmful output. Experiments on 7 mainstream LLMs and three types of benchmark datasets show that Safe2Harm exhibits strong jailbreaking capability, and its overall performance is superior to existing methods. Additionally, we construct a challenging harmful content evaluation dataset containing 358 samples and evaluate the effectiveness of existing harmful detection methods, which can be deployed for LLM input-output filtering to enable defense.

papers.title: Get Out of Jail Free Prompt : How Jailbreaking Compromises Safety in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The increasing popularity of large language models (LLM) has raised important concerns regardingtheir security and the implications of their misuse. This thesis evaluates the vulnerability of LLMs toknown jailbreaking techniques and the potential harm caused by successful attacks. Using a structuredscoring framework, three popular LLMs (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Mistral’s Le Chat) were testedagainst five jailbreaking techniques. All models were susceptible to varying degrees, with DeepSeek-V3 being the most vulnerable, particularly to role-playing. Although most jailbroken responses wereconsidered Low Harm, a few were highly actionable with weak ethical disclaimers, underscoring real-world risks. The thesis emphasizes the importance of prioritizing improved pattern recognition, strictercontextual adherence, and responsible access controls for sensitive capabilities, especially when itcomes to cybersecurity-related content. Until these issues are addressed, jailbreaking will remain athreat requiring proactive and adaptive mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Harmful Prompt Laundering: Jailbreaking LLMs with Abductive Styles and Symbolic Encoding
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, but their potential misuse for harmful purposes remains a significant concern. To strengthen defenses against such vulnerabilities, it is essential to investigate universal jailbreak attacks that exploit intrinsic weaknesses in the architecture and learning paradigms of LLMs. In response, we propose \textbf{H}armful \textbf{P}rompt \textbf{La}undering (HaPLa), a novel and broadly applicable jailbreaking technique that requires only black-box access to target models. HaPLa incorporates two primary strategies: 1) \textit{abductive framing}, which instructs LLMs to infer plausible intermediate steps toward harmful activities, rather than directly responding to explicit harmful queries; and 2) \textit{symbolic encoding}, a lightweight and flexible approach designed to obfuscate harmful content, given that current LLMs remain sensitive primarily to explicit harmful keywords. Experimental results show that HaPLa achieves over 95% attack success rate on GPT-series models and 70% across all targets. Further analysis with diverse symbolic encoding rules also reveals a fundamental challenge: it remains difficult to safely tune LLMs without significantly diminishing their helpfulness in responding to benign queries.

papers.title: Efficient LLM-Jailbreaking via Multimodal-LLM Jailbreak
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on jailbreaking attacks against large language models (LLMs), eliciting them to generate objectionable content in response to harmful user queries. Unlike previous LLM-jailbreak methods that directly orient to LLMs, our approach begins by constructing a multimodal large language model (MLLM) built upon the target LLM. Subsequently, we perform an efficient MLLM jailbreak and obtain a jailbreaking embedding. Finally, we convert the embedding into a textual jailbreaking suffix to carry out the jailbreak of target LLM. Compared to the direct LLM-jailbreak methods, our indirect jailbreaking approach is more efficient, as MLLMs are more vulnerable to jailbreak than pure LLM. Additionally, to improve the attack success rate of jailbreak, we propose an image-text semantic matching scheme to identify a suitable initial input. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art jailbreak methods in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. Moreover, our approach exhibits superior cross-class generalization abilities.

papers.title: A Cross-Language Investigation into Jailbreak Attacks in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular for their advanced text generation capabilities across various domains. However, like any software, they face security challenges, including the risk of 'jailbreak' attacks that manipulate LLMs to produce prohibited content. A particularly underexplored area is the Multilingual Jailbreak attack, where malicious questions are translated into various languages to evade safety filters. Currently, there is a lack of comprehensive empirical studies addressing this specific threat. To address this research gap, we conducted an extensive empirical study on Multilingual Jailbreak attacks. We developed a novel semantic-preserving algorithm to create a multilingual jailbreak dataset and conducted an exhaustive evaluation on both widely-used open-source and commercial LLMs, including GPT-4 and LLaMa. Additionally, we performed interpretability analysis to uncover patterns in Multilingual Jailbreak attacks and implemented a fine-tuning mitigation method. Our findings reveal that our mitigation strategy significantly enhances model defense, reducing the attack success rate by 96.2%. This study provides valuable insights into understanding and mitigating Multilingual Jailbreak attacks.

papers.title: Playing the Fool: Jailbreaking LLMs and Multimodal LLMs with Out-of-Distribution Strategy
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable versatility of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) to generalize across both language and vision tasks, LLMs and MLLMs have shown vulnerability to jailbreaking, generating textual outputs that undermine safety, ethical, and bias standards when exposed to harmful or sensitive inputs. With the recent advancement of safety alignment via preference-tuning from human feedback, LLMs and MLLMs have been equipped with safety guardrails to yield safe, ethical, and fair responses with regard to harmful inputs. However, despite the significance of safety alignment, research on the vulnerabilities remains largely underexplored. In this paper, we investigate the unexplored vulnerability of the safety alignment, examining its ability to consistently provide safety guarantees for out-of-distribution(OOD)-ifying harmful inputs that may fall outside the aligned data distribution. Our key observation is that OOD-ifying the vanilla harmful inputs highly increases the uncertainty of the model to discern the malicious intent within the input, leading to a higher chance of being jailbroken. Exploiting this vulnerability, we propose JOOD, a new Jailbreak framework via OOD-ifying inputs beyond the safety alignment. We explore various off-the-shelf visual and textual transformation techniques for OOD-ifying the harmful inputs. Notably, we observe that even simple mixing-based techniques such as image mixup prove highly effective in increasing the uncertainty of the model, thereby facilitating the bypass of the safety alignment. Experiments across diverse jailbreak scenarios demonstrate that JOOD effectively jailbreaks recent proprietary LLMs and MLLMs such as GPT-4 and o1 with high attack success rate, which previous attack approaches have consistently struggled to jailbreak. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/JOOD.

papers.title: Do Methods to Jailbreak and Defend LLMs Generalize Across Languages?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo safety alignment after training and tuning, yet recent work shows that safety can be bypassed through jailbreak attacks. While many jailbreaks and defenses exist, their cross-lingual generalization remains underexplored. This paper presents the first systematic multilingual evaluation of jailbreaks and defenses across ten languages -- spanning high-, medium-, and low-resource languages -- using six LLMs on HarmBench and AdvBench. We assess two jailbreak types: logical-expression-based and adversarial-prompt-based. For both types, attack success and defense robustness vary across languages: high-resource languages are safer under standard queries but more vulnerable to adversarial ones. Simple defenses can be effective, but are language- and model-dependent. These findings call for language-aware and cross-lingual safety benchmarks for LLMs.

papers.title: Speak Easy: Eliciting Harmful Jailbreaks from LLMs with Simple Interactions
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment efforts, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit harmful behavior. While existing studies predominantly focus on attack methods that require technical expertise, two critical questions remain underexplored: (1) Are jailbroken responses truly useful in enabling average users to carry out harmful actions? (2) Do safety vulnerabilities exist in more common, simple human-LLM interactions? In this paper, we demonstrate that LLM responses most effectively facilitate harmful actions when they are both actionable and informative--two attributes easily elicited in multi-step, multilingual interactions. Using this insight, we propose HarmScore, a jailbreak metric that measures how effectively an LLM response enables harmful actions, and Speak Easy, a simple multi-step, multilingual attack framework. Notably, by incorporating Speak Easy into direct request and jailbreak baselines, we see an average absolute increase of 0.319 in Attack Success Rate and 0.426 in HarmScore in both open-source and proprietary LLMs across four safety benchmarks. Our work reveals a critical yet often overlooked vulnerability: Malicious users can easily exploit common interaction patterns for harmful intentions.

papers.title: Defending LLMs against Jailbreaking Attacks via Backtranslation
papers.abstract: Although many large language models (LLMs) have been trained to refuse harmful requests, they are still vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks which rewrite the original prompt to conceal its harmful intent. In this paper, we propose a new method for defending LLMs against jailbreaking attacks by ``backtranslation''. Specifically, given an initial response generated by the target LLM from an input prompt, our backtranslation prompts a language model to infer an input prompt that can lead to the response. The inferred prompt is called the backtranslated prompt which tends to reveal the actual intent of the original prompt, since it is generated based on the LLM's response and not directly manipulated by the attacker. We then run the target LLM again on the backtranslated prompt, and we refuse the original prompt if the model refuses the backtranslated prompt. We explain that the proposed defense provides several benefits on its effectiveness and efficiency. We empirically demonstrate that our defense significantly outperforms the baselines, in the cases that are hard for the baselines, and our defense also has little impact on the generation quality for benign input prompts.
