papers.research_question: How can jailbreaking attacks on LLMs be enhanced by manipulating the models' attention scores?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttnGCG, an enhanced jailbreaking attack that manipulates LLMs' attention scores to increase focus on adversarial suffixes, leading to higher attack success rates and improved transferability.
papers.conclusion: Attention manipulation is an effective strategy for enhancing jailbreaking attacks on LLMs, and visualizing attention scores offers clear insights into the attack mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
A positive correlation exists between the attention score on the adversarial suffix and the attack success rate (ASR).
AttnGCG consistently outperforms the GCG baseline across various LLMs, achieving an average ASR increase of ~6.3% (GPT-4 judge).
AttnGCG reduces the gap between keyword-based and GPT-4 judge ASR, indicating a reduction in false jailbreaks.
AttnGCG demonstrates strong transferability, improving ASR on unseen harmful goals by an average of 11.4% and on black-box LLMs like GPT-4 by 2.8%.
Attention score visualization provides interpretable insights into how jailbreaking exploits attention distributions.
papers.limitation: The transfer attack performance of AttnGCG is unsatisfactory on the latest models (Gemini-1.5-Pro-latest, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-4o), necessitating further research.
future_direction: Further research to improve transfer attack performance on the latest LLM models.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the vulnerabilities of transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to jailbreaking attacks, focusing specifically on the optimization-based Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) strategy. We first observe a positive correlation between the effectiveness of attacks and the internal behaviors of the models. For instance, attacks tend to be less effective when models pay more attention to system prompts designed to ensure LLM safety alignment. Building on this discovery, we introduce an enhanced method that manipulates models' attention scores to facilitate LLM jailbreaking, which we term AttnGCG. Empirically, AttnGCG shows consistent improvements in attack efficacy across diverse LLMs, achieving an average increase of ~7% in the Llama-2 series and ~10% in the Gemma series. Our strategy also demonstrates robust attack transferability against both unseen harmful goals and black-box LLMs like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Moreover, we note our attention-score visualization is more interpretable, allowing us to gain better insights into how our targeted attention manipulation facilitates more effective jailbreaking. We release the code at https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/AttnGCG-attack.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: NeuroStrike: Neuron-Level Attacks on Aligned LLMs
papers.research_question: How can the sparse, specialized safety neurons introduced by alignment techniques in LLMs be exploited to create effective and generalizable attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroStrike, a neuron-level attack framework that exploits sparse, specialized safety neurons to compromise safety alignment in LLMs, achieving high attack success rates in both white-box (via pruning) and black-box (via profiling) settings.
papers.conclusion: Safety alignment in LLMs is fragile and relies on sparse, attackable safety neurons, posing a significant threat that requires new defensive strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety neurons are sparse (less than 0.6% of neurons in a layer), specialized, and transferable across model variants and families.
Pruning these neurons in white-box models increases the average Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 12.1% to 76.9% across 11 open-source LLMs.
The attack generalizes to multimodal LLMs, achieving 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs after pruning.
Safety neuron transferability enables effective black-box attacks, raising the average ASR from 3.5% to 63.7% across five proprietary models, including Google's Gemini family.
The utility of pruned models on standard NLU benchmarks remains largely intact, indicating targeted degradation of safety mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The white-box attack requires access to model weights and neuron activations.
The black-box attack assumes the availability of a suitable open-weight surrogate model for profiling.
Pruning safety neurons can lead to moderate utility degradation on some reasoning-heavy tasks.
future_direction: Developing defenses against neuron-level attacks.
Improving the robustness of safety alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is critical for the ethical deployment of large language models (LLMs), guiding them to avoid generating harmful or unethical content. Current alignment techniques, such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, remain fragile and can be bypassed by carefully crafted adversarial prompts. Unfortunately, such attacks rely on trial and error, lack generalizability across models, and are constrained by scalability and reliability. This paper presents NeuroStrike, a novel and generalizable attack framework that exploits a fundamental vulnerability introduced by alignment techniques: the reliance on sparse, specialized safety neurons responsible for detecting and suppressing harmful inputs. We apply NeuroStrike to both white-box and black-box settings: In the white-box setting, NeuroStrike identifies safety neurons through feedforward activation analysis and prunes them during inference to disable safety mechanisms. In the black-box setting, we propose the first LLM profiling attack, which leverages safety neuron transferability by training adversarial prompt generators on open-weight surrogate models and then deploying them against black-box and proprietary targets. We evaluate NeuroStrike on over 20 open-weight LLMs from major LLM developers. By removing less than 0.6% of neurons in targeted layers, NeuroStrike achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 76.9% using only vanilla malicious prompts. Moreover, Neurostrike generalizes to four multimodal LLMs with 100% ASR on unsafe image inputs. Safety neurons transfer effectively across architectures, raising ASR to 78.5% on 11 fine-tuned models and 77.7% on five distilled models. The black-box LLM profiling attack achieves an average ASR of 63.7% across five black-box models, including the Google Gemini family.

papers.title: HiddenDetect: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks against Large Vision-Language Models via Monitoring Hidden States
papers.research_question: Can LVLMs detect unsafe prompts through their internal hidden states before generating any output? The paper investigates whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HiddenDetect, a tuning-free framework that detects jailbreak attacks by monitoring refusal semantics in the hidden states of LVLMs, and shows that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns for unsafe prompts.
papers.conclusion: HiddenDetect leverages intrinsic safety signals in LVLM activations to detect jailbreak attacks without tuning, outperforming existing methods and offering a robust and scalable solution for enhancing LVLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, with refusal semantics detectable in hidden states.
Safety activation is delayed for multimodal inputs, especially when harmful intent is conveyed through images, correlating with higher attack success rates.
HiddenDetect achieves higher AUROC than existing state-of-the-art methods on both text-based and multimodal jailbreak benchmarks.
The method is tuning-free, operates directly on internal activations, and generalizes across different LVLM architectures without modification.
The most safety-aware layers are in the middle to late range, and scaling their weights increases the rejection of malicious queries.
papers.limitation:
Relies on the assumption that unsafe prompts consistently induce distinct activation patterns, which may not hold for all adversarial inputs.
Does not actively intervene in response generation, only flags unsafe prompts.
future_direction: Explore adaptive learning mechanisms to dynamically refine detection thresholds.
Integrate activation-based safety monitoring with controlled response modulation.
papers.abstract: The integration of additional modalities increases the susceptibility of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to safety risks, such as jailbreak attacks, compared to their language-only counterparts. While existing research primarily focuses on post-hoc alignment techniques, the underlying safety mechanisms within LVLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work , we investigate whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference. Our findings reveal that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, which can be leveraged to detect and mitigate adversarial inputs without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Building on this insight, we introduce HiddenDetect, a novel tuning-free framework that harnesses internal model activations to enhance safety. Experimental results show that {HiddenDetect} surpasses state-of-the-art methods in detecting jailbreak attacks against LVLMs. By utilizing intrinsic safety-aware patterns, our method provides an efficient and scalable solution for strengthening LVLM robustness against multimodal threats. Our code will be released publicly at https://github.com/leigest519/HiddenDetect.

papers.title: Multi-Turn Jailbreaking Large Language Models via Attention Shifting
papers.research_question: What are the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs, and how can attention shifting be leveraged to improve such attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ASJA, a multi-turn jailbreak method that shifts LLM attention away from harmful keywords by fabricating dialogue history using a genetic algorithm, achieving higher attack success rates and stealthiness.
papers.conclusion: ASJA effectively breaks the LLM's safety alignment by shifting attention to historical queries and responses via fabricated dialogue, outperforming baselines in effectiveness, stealthiness, and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
Successful multi-turn jailbreaks shift LLM attention away from harmful keywords to dialogue history, especially previous responses.
ASJA achieves higher attack success rates (44.91% improvement in harmfulness and 34.02% in relevance) compared to baselines.
ASJA maintains stealthiness (low perplexity) and has good transferability to other models.
The attention on harmful keywords in the last query is significantly lower in successful jailbreaks.
Optimizing both queries and responses in dialogue history is more effective than optimizing queries alone.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved significant performance in various natural language processing tasks but also pose safety and ethical threats, thus requiring red teaming and alignment processes to bolster their safety. To effectively exploit these aligned LLMs, recent studies have introduced jailbreak attacks based on multi-turn dialogues. These attacks aim to prompt LLMs to generate harmful or biased content by guiding them through contextual content. However, the underlying reasons for the effectiveness of multi-turn jailbreaks remain unclear. Existing attacks often focus on optimizing queries and escalating toxicity to construct dialogues, lacking a thorough analysis of the inherent vulnerabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis of the differences between single-turn and multi-turn jailbreaks and find that successful multi-turn jailbreaks can effectively disperse the attention of LLMs on keywords associated with harmful behaviors, especially in historical responses. Based on this, we propose ASJA, a new multi-turn jailbreak approach by shifting the attention of LLMs, specifically by iteratively fabricating the dialogue history through a genetic algorithm to induce LLMs to generate harmful content. Extensive experiments on three LLMs and two datasets show that our approach surpasses existing approaches in jailbreak effectiveness, the stealth of jailbreak prompts, and attack efficiency. Our work emphasizes the importance of enhancing the robustness of LLMs' attention mechanism in multi-turn dialogue scenarios for a better defense strategy.

papers.title: Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications
papers.research_question: What is the brittleness of safety alignment in large language models, and can it be explained by sparse safety-critical regions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that safety-critical regions in aligned LLMs are sparse and can be isolated via neuron and rank attribution methods, leading to brittleness in safety mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The brittleness of safety alignment stems from sparse safety-critical regions, highlighting the need for more robust safety strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-critical neurons and ranks are sparse, comprising about 3% and 2.5% respectively.
Removing these regions compromises safety while preserving utility.
Models remain vulnerable to fine-tuning attacks even when safety-critical regions are frozen.
Pruning least safety-relevant neurons can enhance safety against adversarial attacks.
Disentanglement methods (set difference and orthogonal projection) effectively isolate safety-critical regions.
papers.limitation: Potential misuse by malicious actors to remove safety guardrails from models.
future_direction: Development of more robust safety alignment algorithms that integrate safety-critical regions seamlessly with utility regions.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show inherent brittleness in their safety mechanisms, as evidenced by their susceptibility to jailbreaking and even non-malicious fine-tuning. This study explores this brittleness of safety alignment by leveraging pruning and low-rank modifications. We develop methods to identify critical regions that are vital for safety guardrails, and that are disentangled from utility-relevant regions at both the neuron and rank levels. Surprisingly, the isolated regions we find are sparse, comprising about $3\%$ at the parameter level and $2.5\%$ at the rank level. Removing these regions compromises safety without significantly impacting utility, corroborating the inherent brittleness of the model's safety mechanisms. Moreover, we show that LLMs remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted. These findings underscore the urgent need for more robust safety strategies in LLMs.

papers.title: Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to build inherently interpretable large language models (LLMs) for text classification and text generation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models (CB-LLMs), a framework to build inherently interpretable LLMs for text classification and generation that matches black-box model performance while providing transparency and control.
papers.conclusion: CB-LLMs provide a framework for building interpretable LLMs without sacrificing performance, enabling transparent reasoning, controlled generation, and enhanced safety and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
CB-LLMs for text classification achieve accuracy competitive with or superior to black-box models and provide faithful explanations as measured by human evaluation.
CB-LLMs for text generation match black-box performance and enable controllable generation, including toxicity reduction through neuron steering.
The method scales to large datasets (e.g., 560k samples) and automates concept labeling without expensive LLM API calls.
Human evaluations show CB-LLMs provide better explanations than prior interpretable models (TBM & C3M).
Concept unlearning in CB-LLMs can improve prediction fairness by removing biased or subjective concepts.
papers.abstract: We introduce Concept Bottleneck Large Language Models (CB-LLMs), a novel framework for building inherently interpretable Large Language Models (LLMs). In contrast to traditional black-box LLMs that rely on limited post-hoc interpretations, CB-LLMs integrate intrinsic interpretability directly into the LLMs -- allowing accurate explanations with scalability and transparency. We build CB-LLMs for two essential NLP tasks: text classification and text generation. In text classification, CB-LLMs is competitive with, and at times outperforms, traditional black-box models while providing explicit and interpretable reasoning. For the more challenging task of text generation, interpretable neurons in CB-LLMs enable precise concept detection, controlled generation, and safer outputs. The embedded interpretability empowers users to transparently identify harmful content, steer model behavior, and unlearn undesired concepts -- significantly enhancing the safety, reliability, and trustworthiness of LLMs, which are critical capabilities notably absent in existing models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/CB-LLMs.

papers.title: What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs? Investigating the Mechanisms Behind Attacks
papers.research_question: What features in prompts lead to successful jailbreaks in LLMs, and are they linear or non-linear?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak features in LLMs are non-linear and model-specific, and non-linear probes can guide effective latent-space interventions to increase or decrease jailbreak success.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak mechanisms are heterogeneous and non-linear, and the proposed methodology provides insights into the features driving jailbreak outcomes.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on prompt representations can predict jailbreak success with high accuracy.
Non-linear probes generalize better across layers than linear probes.
Jailbreak features are not universal; probes do not generalize well to unseen attack types.
Non-linear probe-guided interventions can effectively increase or decrease jailbreak success.
Features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaks have been a central focus of research regarding the safety and reliability of large language models (LLMs), yet the mechanisms underlying these attacks remain poorly understood. While previous studies have predominantly relied on linear methods to detect jailbreak attempts and model refusals, we take a different approach by examining both linear and non-linear features in prompts that lead to successful jailbreaks. First, we introduce a novel dataset comprising 10,800 jailbreak attempts spanning 35 diverse attack methods. Leveraging this dataset, we train linear and non-linear probes on hidden states of open-weight LLMs to predict jailbreak success. Probes achieve strong in-distribution accuracy but transfer is attack-family-specific, revealing that different jailbreaks are supported by distinct internal mechanisms rather than a single universal direction. To establish causal relevance, we construct probe-guided latent interventions that systematically shift compliance in the predicted direction. Interventions derived from non-linear probes produce larger and more reliable effects than those from linear probes, indicating that features linked to jailbreak success are encoded non-linearly in prompt representations. Overall, the results surface heterogeneous, non-linear structure in jailbreak mechanisms and provide a prompt-side methodology for recovering and testing the features that drive jailbreak outcomes.

papers.title: The Emergence of Abstract Thought in Large Language Models Beyond Any Language
papers.research_question: Do LLMs think in the distinct space of each language, or do they operate in a higher-level language-agnostic space beyond any specific language? Does the trend of non-English performance compared to English indicate the emergence of abstract thought within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space (shared neurons) that underlies generalization across languages and supports abstract thought. Based on this, neuron-specific training strategies are proposed to enhance multilingual capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Shared neurons form a compact, language-agnostic set that supports abstract reasoning across languages, and neuron-specific training strategies can enhance multilingual performance.
papers.key_findings:
The proportion of language-shared neurons increases with model evolution and correlates with multilingual ability.
Language-shared neurons become more functionally important than language-exclusive neurons, evolving into language-agnostic neurons that support abstract thought.
Neuron-targeted training based on the language-agnostic score effectively improves multilingual performance, with different strategies for models at different developmental stages.
papers.limitation: Limited by computational resources, restricting evaluation on larger LLMs and full exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
future_direction: Evaluation on larger LLMs and exploration of neuron-centric training at larger scales.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance, their capacity to function effectively across a diverse range of languages has shown marked improvement. Preliminary studies observe that the hidden activations of LLMs often resemble English, even when responding to non-English prompts. This has led to the widespread assumption that LLMs may "think" in English. However, more recent results showing strong multilingual performance, even surpassing English performance on specific tasks in other languages, challenge this view. In this work, we find that LLMs progressively develop a core language-agnostic parameter space-a remarkably small subset of parameters whose deactivation results in significant performance degradation across all languages. This compact yet critical set of parameters underlies the model's ability to generalize beyond individual languages, supporting the emergence of abstract thought that is not tied to any specific linguistic system. Specifically, we identify language-related neurons-those are consistently activated during the processing of particular languages, and categorize them as either shared (active across multiple languages) or exclusive (specific to one). As LLMs undergo continued development over time, we observe a marked increase in both the proportion and functional importance of shared neurons, while exclusive neurons progressively diminish in influence. These shared neurons constitute the backbone of the core language-agnostic parameter space, supporting the emergence of abstract thought. Motivated by these insights, we propose neuron-specific training strategies tailored to LLMs' language-agnostic levels at different development stages. Experiments across diverse LLM families support our approach.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression: From Language-Specific to Shared Neurons
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models achieve cross-lingual generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, with representations evolving from language-specific to shared cross-lingual abstractions, demonstrated via neuron analysis and manipulation.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual generalization in multilingual language models emerges through compression during pre-training, leading to the development of shared concept neurons across languages that encode generalized semantic representations.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models initially form language-specific representations which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.
Language identification probing reveals a shift from uniform capabilities across layers to specialized layer functions, with middle layers becoming more language-agnostic.
Specific neurons emerge as reliable predictors for the same semantic concepts across different languages, showing increasing alignment during training.
Neuron manipulation experiments demonstrate that concept-specific neurons identified from one language can guide semantically coherent text generation in another language once cross-lingual generalization is achieved.
The model's internal representations encode shared conceptual knowledge independent of the original language encoding.
papers.limitation: The number of publicly available training checkpoints for the BLOOM models is limited, restricting the granularity of analysis.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to transfer knowledge across languages, despite being trained without explicit cross-lingual supervision.We analyze the parameter spaces of three MLLMs to study how their representations evolve during pre-training, observing patterns consistent with compression: models initially form language-specific representations, which gradually converge into cross-lingual abstractions as training progresses.Through probing experiments, we observe a clear transition from uniform language identification capabilities across layers to more specialized layer functions.For deeper analysis, we focus on neurons that encode distinct semantic concepts.By tracing their development during pre-training, we show how they gradually align across languages.Notably, we identify specific neurons that emerge as increasingly reliable predictors for the same concepts across languages.This alignment manifests concretely in generation: once an MLLM exhibits cross-lingual generalization according to our measures, we can select concept-specific neurons identified from, e.g., Spanish text and manipulate them to guide token predictions.Remarkably, rather than generating Spanish text, the model produces semantically coherent English text.This demonstrates that cross-lingually aligned neurons encode generalized semantic representations, independent of the original language encoding.

papers.title: SCANS: Mitigating the Exaggerated Safety for LLMs via Safety-Conscious Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned Large Language Models (LLMs) that cause false refusal of benign queries, without compromising their defense capability against harmful queries?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SCANS, a training-free activation steering method that extracts refusal steering vectors from model hidden states and steers activations in safety-critical layers to reduce false refusal on benign queries while maintaining refusal on harmful ones.
papers.conclusion: SCANS effectively mitigates the exaggerated safety issue in aligned LLMs through activation steering in safety-critical layers, balancing helpfulness and harmlessness without significant degradation of general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
SCANS significantly reduces the false refusal rate on safe prompts (e.g., by 24.7% on XSTest and 26.3% on OKTest on average) without compromising adequate safety on harmful prompts.
The method identifies middle layers as safety-critical for steering, as vocabulary projection of steering vectors from these layers promotes refusal-related tokens.
SCANS has minimal impact on general model capabilities (perplexity, summarization, QA accuracy) and requires minor extra inference cost.
A similarity-based classification method using hidden state transitions effectively distinguishes harmful from benign queries, achieving high F1 scores.
The performance of SCANS is robust across different model sizes and architectures, including Llama2, Vicuna, Qwen, Llama3, and Gemma2.
papers.limitation:
Classification inaccuracy in the steering direction identification can lead to a slight drop in refusal rate on unsafe prompts.
Comparison experiments on larger-scale models (>13B parameters) were limited to one prompt engineering baseline due to computational constraints and time.
Applying too large a steering multiplier (α) can sometimes result in nonsense or repetitive outputs.
future_direction: Improving the classification method for more accurate harmfulness detection.
Conducting more comprehensive comparison experiments on larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is indispensable for Large Language Models (LLMs) to defend threats from malicious instructions. However, recent researches reveal safety-aligned LLMs prone to reject benign queries due to the exaggerated safety issue, limiting their helpfulness. In this paper, we propose a Safety-Conscious Activation Steering (SCANS) method to mitigate the exaggerated safety concerns in aligned LLMs. First, SCANS extracts the refusal steering vectors within the activation space and utilizes vocabulary projection to anchor some specific safety-critical layers which influence model refusal behavior. Second, by tracking the hidden state transition, SCANS identifies the steering direction and steers the model behavior accordingly, achieving a balance between exaggerated safety and adequate safety. Experiments show that SCANS achieves new state-of-the-art performance on XSTest and OKTest benchmarks, without impairing their defense capability against harmful queries and maintaining almost unchanged model capability.

papers.title: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations
papers.research_question: Why does jailbreak transferability occur? Is it due to shared representations or incidental flaws?
papers.core_contribution: Jailbreak transferability emerges from shared representations, and increasing representational similarity through benign-only distillation causally increases transfer.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak transfer is reframed as a consequence of representation alignment rather than an incidental byproduct of safety training.
papers.key_findings:
Representational similarity and jailbreak strength on the source model are two factors that systematically shape transferability.
Distilling a target model on benign data from a source model increases their representational similarity and causally increases jailbreak transferability.
Persona-style jailbreaks transfer more reliably than cipher-based jailbreaks, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit shared representation space.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak transferability is the surprising phenomenon when an adversarial attack compromising one model also elicits harmful responses from other models. Despite widespread demonstrations, there is little consensus on why transfer is possible: is it a quirk of safety training, an artifact of model families, or a more fundamental property of representation learning? We present evidence that transferability emerges from shared representations rather than incidental flaws. Across 20 open-weight models and 33 jailbreak attacks, we find two factors that systematically shape transfer: (1) representational similarity under benign prompts, and (2) the strength of the jailbreak on the source model. To move beyond correlation, we show that deliberately increasing similarity through benign only distillation causally increases transfer. Our qualitative analyses reveal systematic transferability patterns across different types of jailbreaks. For example, persona-style jailbreaks transfer far more often than cipher-based prompts, consistent with the idea that natural-language attacks exploit models' shared representation space, whereas cipher-based attacks rely on idiosyncratic quirks that do not generalize. Together, these results reframe jailbreak transfer as a consequence of representation alignment rather than a fragile byproduct of safety training.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Safety Mechanism Transfer in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: Why does the safety mechanism for text in LLMs fail to transfer to vision in LVLMs, and how can we address this?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel text-guided vision-language alignment method (TGA) that transfers safety mechanisms from text to vision by aligning hidden states, and provides an analysis showing that insufficient alignment at hidden states causes the safety mechanism transfer failure.
papers.conclusion: TGA effectively transfers safety mechanisms from text to vision by aligning hidden states, and maintains general performance on vision tasks, providing a safe and effective vision-language alignment method.
papers.key_findings:
Existing vision-language alignment methods fail to transfer safety mechanisms from text to vision, leading to vulnerabilities in LVLMs for toxic images.
Safety mechanism activation in LVLMs occurs at specific transformer layers and is driven by hidden states of toxic tokens.
Insufficient alignment of hidden states between vision and language at these layers causes the safety mechanism to fail for vision.
The proposed TGA method successfully transfers safety mechanisms to vision without safety fine-tuning and maintains general vision task performance.
TGA improves safety performance on toxic images and is robust to caption errors and jailbreak attacks.
papers.limitation: The method may fail for images with harmful objects that are not easily noticed, images in specific domains (e.g., bloody), and images that are hard for the LVLM to understand.
papers.abstract: Vision-language alignment in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) successfully enables LLMs to understand visual input. However, we find that existing vision-language alignment methods fail to transfer the existing safety mechanism for text in LLMs to vision, which leads to vulnerabilities in toxic image. To explore the cause of this problem, we give the insightful explanation of where and how the safety mechanism of LVLMs operates and conduct comparative analysis between text and vision. We find that the hidden states at the specific transformer layers play a crucial role in the successful activation of safety mechanism, while the vision-language alignment at hidden states level in current methods is insufficient. This results in a semantic shift for input images compared to text in hidden states, therefore misleads the safety mechanism. To address this, we propose a novel Text-Guided vision-language Alignment method (TGA) for LVLMs. TGA retrieves the texts related to input vision and uses them to guide the projection of vision into the hidden states space in LLMs. Experiments show that TGA not only successfully transfers the safety mechanism for text in basic LLMs to vision in vision-language alignment for LVLMs without any safety fine-tuning on the visual modality but also maintains the general performance on various vision tasks (Safe and Good).

papers.title: Linearly Decoding Refused Knowledge in Aligned Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent is potentially harmful information decodable from innocuous hidden states without the use of jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: Instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space; it merely suppresses its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.
papers.conclusion: Instruction-tuning suppresses generative access to harmful information but does not remove it from representations, leaving it linearly decodable and influential in downstream behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover jailbroken responses from innocuous hidden states with high Pearson correlations (e.g., >0.8 for average IQ of countries).
Probes trained on base models transfer to instruction-tuned models, indicating that representations of refused information persist through instruction-tuning.
Probe-predicted values correlate with model-generated pairwise comparisons (Spearman correlations up to 0.824), suggesting that the decoded information aligns with suppressed generative behavior.
Not all attributes are linearly decodable; performance varies by entity type and model size, with larger models showing better decodability.
Jailbreak-specific probing sometimes improves performance but not always, and can even degrade due to overfitting or stylistic entanglement.
papers.limitation:
Not every attribute is linearly predictable from hidden states; performance varies across entity types and attributes.
The study is limited to four entity types and three open-source LMs, which may not be representative.
The attributes studied are not factually grounded and may be ill-defined or impossible to measure reliably.
papers.abstract: Most commonly used language models (LMs) are instruction-tuned and aligned using a combination of fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, causing them to refuse users requests deemed harmful by the model. However, jailbreak prompts can often bypass these refusal mechanisms and elicit harmful responses. In this work, we study the extent to which information accessed via jailbreak prompts is decodable using linear probes trained on LM hidden states. We show that a great deal of initially refused information is linearly decodable. For example, across models, the response of a jailbroken LM for the average IQ of a country can be predicted by a linear probe with Pearson correlations exceeding $0.8$. Surprisingly, we find that probes trained on base models (which do not refuse) sometimes transfer to their instruction-tuned versions and are capable of revealing information that jailbreaks decode generatively, suggesting that the internal representations of many refused properties persist from base LMs through instruction-tuning. Importantly, we show that this information is not merely "leftover" in instruction-tuned models, but is actively used by them: we find that probe-predicted values correlate with LM generated pairwise comparisons, indicating that the information decoded by our probes align with suppressed generative behavior that may be expressed more subtly in other downstream tasks. Overall, our results suggest that instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space-they merely suppress its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.

papers.title: Measuring Impacts of Poisoning on Model Parameters and Neuron Activations: A Case Study of Poisoning CodeBERT
papers.research_question: Can hidden backdoor signals be detected in poisoned code models by analyzing attention weights, biases, activation values, and context embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that in poisoned CodeBERT models, activation values and context embeddings exhibit noticeable patterns for poisoned samples, while attention weights and biases show no significant differences, contributing to white-box backdoor detection.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that activation values and context embeddings can indicate backdoor signals in poisoned CodeBERT models, but attention weights and biases do not show significant differences.
papers.key_findings:
Activation values of poisoned samples in the poisoned CodeBERT model are grouped into a single cluster in upper encoder layers, unlike in lower layers.
Context embeddings of poisoned samples from the poisoned model form distinct clusters based on the applied triggers, while clean samples are randomly scattered.
Attention weights and biases do not show significant differences between clean and poisoned CodeBERT models.
Poisoned fine-tuning incurs more changes on attention key biases compared to clean fine-tuning when compared to pre-trained parameters.
Resetting fine-tuned attention weights to pre-trained weights based on thresholds reduces both accuracy and attack success rate, providing no clear backdoor signal.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on CodeBERT and may not generalize to other models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other code models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized software development practices, yet concerns about their safety have arisen, particularly regarding hidden backdoors, aka trojans. Backdoor attacks involve the insertion of triggers into training data, allowing attackers to manipulate the behavior of the model maliciously. In this paper, we focus on analyzing the model parameters to detect potential backdoor signals in code models. Specifically, we examine attention weights and biases, activation values, and context embeddings of the clean and poisoned CodeBERT models. Our results suggest noticeable patterns in activation values and context embeddings of poisoned samples for the poisoned CodeBERT model; however, attention weights and biases do not show any significant differences. This work contributes to ongoing efforts in white-box detection of backdoor signals in LLMs of code through the analysis of parameters and activations.

papers.title: Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?
papers.research_question: Do internal layers of LLMs reveal patterns for jailbreak detection? Specifically, how do hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that analyzing internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts.
papers.conclusion: Examining internal layer representations of LLMs combined with tensor decomposition techniques provides a promising approach for detecting jailbreak prompts, offering a simple, efficient, and effective pathway for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
For GPT-J, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) representations outperform layer outputs for jailbreak classification.
For Mamba-2, Mixer representations outperform Block outputs for jailbreak classification.
Tensor decomposition of internal representations yields latent factors that provide clear separation between jailbreak and benign prompts.
A simple pipeline of tensor decomposition followed by basic classifiers (e.g., Random Forest, SVM) achieves effective jailbreak detection.
papers.limitation: The study is preliminary and requires further work on larger datasets, additional architectures, and more sophisticated evaluation settings.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to larger datasets.
Apply the methodology to additional architectures.
Conduct more sophisticated evaluation.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a pressing concern with the increasing prevalence and accessibility of conversational LLMs. Adversarial users often exploit these models through carefully engineered prompts to elicit restricted or sensitive outputs, a strategy widely referred to as jailbreaking. While numerous defense mechanisms have been proposed, attackers continuously develop novel prompting techniques, and no existing model can be considered fully resistant. In this study, we investigate the jailbreak phenomenon by examining the internal representations of LLMs, with a focus on how hidden layers respond to jailbreak versus benign prompts. Specifically, we analyze the open-source LLM GPT-J and the state-space model Mamba2, presenting preliminary findings that highlight distinct layer-wise behaviors. Our results suggest promising directions for further research on leveraging internal model dynamics for robust jailbreak detection and defense.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: SoK: a Comprehensive Causality Analysis Framework for Large Language Model Security
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis be used to understand and mitigate vulnerabilities, such as jailbreaks, in Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified causality analysis framework for LLM security that enables multi-level causal investigation (token, neuron, layer, representation) and demonstrates its effectiveness in understanding and defending against jailbreaks and other threats.
papers.conclusion: The causality analysis framework bridges theoretical causality and practical model safety, establishing a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Targeted interventions on causally critical components (tokens, neurons, layers, representations) can reliably modify model safety behavior.
Safety mechanisms are highly localized in early-to-middle transformer layers (2-12), with only 1-2% of neurons exhibiting causal influence.
Causal features extracted from the multi-level analysis achieve over 95% detection accuracy across jailbreak, hallucination, backdoor, and fairness tasks.
Token-level causal influence is high for optimization-based attacks (e.g., GCG) but low for semantically distributed attacks (e.g., AutoDAN).
Representation-level interventions via geometric steering along the acceptance direction are highly effective at crossing safety decision boundaries.
future_direction: Extending the causality analysis framework to multimodal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Discovering additional causally relevant components or signals within LLMs that may reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
Conducting rigorous, comparative studies of existing causality-based approaches to evaluate their effectiveness and generalizability.
Developing more advanced causality-informed defenses that combine multi-level interventions or dynamically adapt safety mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities but remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking, where crafted prompts bypass safety mechanisms. Understanding the causal factors behind such vulnerabilities is essential for building reliable defenses. In this work, we introduce a unified causality analysis framework that systematically supports all levels of causal investigation in LLMs, ranging from token-level, neuron-level, and layer-level interventions to representation-level analysis. The framework enables consistent experimentation and comparison across diverse causality-based attack and defense methods. Accompanying this implementation, we provide the first comprehensive survey of causality-driven jailbreak studies and empirically evaluate the framework on multiple open-weight models and safety-critical benchmarks including jailbreaks, hallucination detection, backdoor identification, and fairness evaluation. Our results reveal that: (1) targeted interventions on causally critical components can reliably modify safety behavior; (2) safety-related mechanisms are highly localized (i.e., concentrated in early-to-middle layers with only 1--2\% of neurons exhibiting causal influence); and (3) causal features extracted from our framework achieve over 95\% detection accuracy across multiple threat types. By bridging theoretical causality analysis and practical model safety, our framework establishes a reproducible foundation for research on causality-based attacks, interpretability, and robust attack detection and mitigation in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/Amadeuszhao/SOK_Casuality.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons Do Not Facilitate Cross-Lingual Transfer
papers.research_question: This work explores whether existing techniques to identify language-specific neurons can be leveraged to enhance cross-lingual task performance of low-resource languages.
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that test-time interventions and fine-tuning of language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs are insufficient to yield meaningful improvements in cross-lingual task performance for low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific neurons do not function independently but interact with broader model components, and need further investigation as tools of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Test-time interventions on language-specific neurons do not improve cross-lingual task performance and often disrupt task-relevant information.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons using LoRA does not lead to significant improvements in downstream task performance.
Setting neuron activations to zero does not significantly degrade task performance, suggesting zero is not a true indicator of deactivation.
Language-specific neurons are polysemantic and not independent, which limits the effectiveness of targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on language-specific neurons in the MLP layers, excluding attention mechanisms which may also play a significant role.
Experiments use a limited number of languages and datasets, limiting generalizability.
Interventions rely on statistical activations computed from Wikipedia text, which might not fully capture task-specific behavior.
Does not explore alternate methods of fine-tuning techniques that might yield better results.

papers.title: False Sense of Security: Why Probing-based Malicious Input Detection Fails to Generalize
papers.research_question: Do probing classifiers for LLM safety detection learn semantic harmfulness or rely on superficial patterns?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that probing classifiers for LLM safety detection rely on superficial patterns like instructional formats and trigger words, rather than semantic understanding of harmfulness, leading to poor out-of-distribution performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that current probing-based safety detection methods provide a false sense of security by relying on spurious correlations, and calls for more robust approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Probing classifiers achieve near-perfect in-distribution accuracy but fail dramatically on out-of-distribution data.
Simple n-gram methods achieve comparable performance to probing classifiers, suggesting reliance on surface-level patterns.
Classifiers perform poorly on semantically cleaned datasets where harmful content is replaced with benign alternatives.
Probing classifiers depend on instructional patterns and trigger words rather than semantic harmfulness.
LLMs themselves possess zero-shot safety classification ability, but probing classifiers cannot leverage this effectively.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets, which may not generalize to other languages and cultural contexts.
Analysis is restricted to decoder-only transformer models, leaving other architectures unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can comply with harmful instructions, raising serious safety concerns despite their impressive capabilities. Recent work has leveraged probing-based approaches to study the separability of malicious and benign inputs in LLMs' internal representations, and researchers have proposed using such probing methods for safety detection. We systematically re-examine this paradigm. Motivated by poor out-of-distribution performance, we hypothesize that probes learn superficial patterns rather than semantic harmfulness. Through controlled experiments, we confirm this hypothesis and identify the specific patterns learned: instructional patterns and trigger words. Our investigation follows a systematic approach, progressing from demonstrating comparable performance of simple n-gram methods, to controlled experiments with semantically cleaned datasets, to detailed analysis of pattern dependencies. These results reveal a false sense of security around current probing-based approaches and highlight the need to redesign both models and evaluation protocols, for which we provide further discussions in the hope of suggesting responsible further research in this direction. We have open-sourced the project at https://github.com/WangCheng0116/Why-Probe-Fails.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: Redefining Experts: Interpretable Decomposition of Language Models for Toxicity Mitigation
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the reliability of individual neurons as toxicity indicators, the advantages of layer-wise representations for toxicity detection, and interpretable mechanisms for toxic generation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EigenShift, a novel method for toxicity mitigation that uses eigen-decomposition of the language model's final linear layer to target and suppress generation-aligned components responsible for toxic outputs, reducing toxicity with minimal impact on linguistic competence.
papers.conclusion: The work challenges the neuron-centric paradigm for toxicity mitigation and proposes EigenShift, an interpretable, minimally invasive method based on eigen-decomposition of the final layer, which effectively reduces toxic generation while preserving model fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons are unreliable indicators of toxicity, with most performing near random chance.
Aggregated layer-wise representations provide more robust and stable signals for toxicity detection than single neurons.
The proposed EigenShift method reduces toxicity by 58% while only increasing perplexity by 3.62%, achieving a TPH score of 60.37%.
EigenShift outperforms prior intervention baselines in balancing toxicity reduction and perplexity preservation across multiple language models.
The method successfully disentangles and targets generation experts while preserving detection experts, avoiding catastrophic forgetting of language abilities.
papers.limitation: The current work does not explore a layer-wise decomposition of LLMs, such as distinguishing between early, middle, and final layers in terms of their contribution to semantic choices.
future_direction: Investigating how semantic eigen-directions evolve or emerge across different layers of the model for deeper interpretability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive fluency across diverse tasks, yet their tendency to produce toxic content remains a critical challenge for AI safety and public trust. Existing toxicity mitigation approaches primarily manipulate individual neuron activations, but these methods suffer from instability, context dependence, and often compromise the model's core language abilities. To address these shortcomings, we investigate three key questions: the stability of neuron-level toxicity indicators, the advantages of structural (layer-wise) representations, and the interpretability of mechanisms driving toxic generation. Through extensive experiments on Jigsaw and ToxiCN datasets, we show that aggregated layer-wise features provide more robust signals than single neurons. Moreover, we observe conceptual limitations in prior works that conflate toxicity detection experts and generation experts within neuron-based interventions. To mitigate this, we propose a novel principled intervention technique, EigenShift, based on eigen-decomposition of the language model's final output layer. This method selectively targets generation-aligned components, enabling precise toxicity suppression without impairing linguistic competence. Our method requires no additional training or fine-tuning, incurs minimal computational cost, and is grounded in rigorous theoretical analysis.

papers.title: What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning? A Mechanistic Study
papers.research_question: What is the safety mechanism learned by the model via safety fine-tuning, and how are jailbreak and adversarial attacks able to bypass this mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Safety fine-tuning methods minimally transform MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, causing clustering of safe and unsafe activations; jailbreaks bypass safety by having activations similar to safe samples.
papers.conclusion: Safety fine-tuning minimally transforms MLP weights to project unsafe inputs into the null space, leading to clustering; jailbreaks bypass this by having activations similar to safe samples. This mechanistic understanding can inform more robust safety fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety fine-tuning leads to separate clusters of activations for safe and unsafe samples.
The transformation ∆W has its column-space aligned with the null-space of the instruction fine-tuned weights, making it orthogonal to the original weights.
∆W preferentially impacts unsafe samples, as their pre-activations have larger projection onto the row-space of ∆W.
The local Lipschitzness of the model decreases for unsafe samples after safety fine-tuning, making the model less sensitive to perturbations on unsafe inputs.
Jailbreak attacks (competing objectives, mismatched generalization, adversarial embeddings) have activations that are closer to safe samples, thus bypassing the safety mechanism.
future_direction: Using ∆W from stronger safety fine-tuning methods to improve weaker ones
Designing more robust safety fine-tuning protocols based on the mechanistic understanding
papers.abstract: Safety fine-tuning helps align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences for their safe deployment. To better understand the underlying factors that make models safe via safety fine-tuning, we design a synthetic data generation framework that captures salient aspects of an unsafe input by modeling the interaction between the task the model is asked to perform (e.g., "design") versus the specific concepts the task is asked to be performed upon (e.g., a "cycle" vs. a "bomb"). Using this, we investigate three well-known safety fine-tuning methods -- supervised safety fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and unlearning -- and provide significant evidence demonstrating that these methods minimally transform MLP weights to specifically align unsafe inputs into its weights' null space. This yields a clustering of inputs based on whether the model deems them safe or not. Correspondingly, when an adversarial input (e.g., a jailbreak) is provided, its activations are closer to safer samples, leading to the model processing such an input as if it were safe. We validate our findings, wherever possible, on real-world models -- specifically, Llama-2 7B and Llama-3 8B.
